ideas.title: Writing

date.marks: The earliest proto-cuneiform tablets (Uruk IV phase)
date.note: 3200 BCE is a conventional date. Almost all of the earliest tablets were found in rubbish deposits that cannot be dated precisely [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 34]. Writing appeared at roughly the same time in Egypt [@woods-2010-intro, p. 15].

ideas.summary: Administrators in Uruk, arguably the world's first city, begin recording goods and labour on clay tablets. Writing starts as a tool of bureaucracy, not literature, and is invented independently at least four times: in Mesopotamia, Egypt, China and Mesoamerica.
ideas.body:
**The first city.** In the Late Uruk period (c. 3350–3100 BCE), Uruk grew to 20,000–50,000 people and became "arguably, the world's first true city." The new administration needed to track production, goods and labour, and writing was invented in that setting [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 34].

**Precursors.** Before writing, Near Eastern administrators kept accounts with small clay tokens, some sealed inside clay envelopes ("bullae"). That the tokens were forerunners of the earliest tablets, first argued by Denise Schmandt-Besserat, is "core knowledge" among cuneiformists. Many of the numerical signs on early tablets match the tokens in form and function [@englund-2004, p. 100].

**Dating.** The earliest tablets fall into two script phases: Uruk IV (c. 3200 BCE) and Uruk III (c. 3100 BCE). The German Archaeological Institute excavated about 5,000 proto-cuneiform tablets at Uruk between 1928 and 1976 [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 35]. The whole proto-cuneiform corpus runs to over 6,000 tablets and fragments [@englund-2004, p. 100].

**Purpose.** Nearly all the earliest texts are administrative. Literature, religious texts, historical documents and letters appear only from the mid-third millennium BCE, some 700 years after the first written evidence [@woods-2010-mesopotamia, p. 34].

**Independent inventions.** There are four "pristine" writing systems, invented with no knowledge of writing elsewhere: Mesopotamia and Egypt at the end of the fourth millennium BCE, China at the end of the second millennium BCE, and Mesoamerica by the middle of the first millennium BCE [@woods-2010-intro, p. 15].

ideas.title: Royal sun temples of the Fifth Dynasty

date.marks: Approximate start of Userkaf's reign, the first king credited with building a sun temple; the temple's construction date itself is not fixed.
date.note: Old Kingdom absolute dates vary by chronology. Magli and Bárta (via Archaeology magazine) give Userkaf's reign as about 2465–2458 BCE [@magli-2009, PDF p. 6; @archaeology-sun-kings-2020, founder paragraph], while UCL's Digital Egypt dates the dynasty to 2450–2300 BCE [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text].

ideas.origin: Userkaf, Fifth Dynasty Egypt (Abu Ghurab, near Abusir)
ideas.summary: Userkaf, founder of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty, is credited as the first king to build a sun temple to Ra, at Abu Ghurab, in addition to his pyramid. How many later kings did the same is debated.
ideas.body:
Userkaf, first king of the Fifth Dynasty, is described by UCL's Digital Egypt as "the first king who built a sun temple to support his eternal cult". His temple at Abu Ghurab, called Nekhen-Re, is known from excavation reports by Ricke and Edel [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text]. Besides it, he was buried in a pyramid at Saqqara [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text]. The idea is therefore a second royal monument, devoted to the sun god, built beside the pyramid. Magli also calls Userkaf's the first sun temple in the Abu Gorab zone. He describes a lower building and an access ramp leading up to a monumental area, where a stone base carried a high, non-monolithic obelisk. He suggests the plan was probably a copy of the temple at Heliopolis [@magli-2009, PDF p. 6].

Scholars read the purpose in different ways. Miroslav Bárta, in a magazine interview, says the Fifth Dynasty temples were dedicated to Ra and linked the pharaoh's authority to the sun god's supremacy [@archaeology-sun-kings-2020, founder paragraph]. He adds that offerings for royal mortuary complexes were first taken to the temples to be exposed to the sun before going on to the mortuary temples [@archaeology-sun-kings-2020, six-temples paragraph]. Magli proposes instead that such temples signalled the king's link with the sun god when his pyramid's location did not already show it [@magli-2009, PDF p. 11]. This second reading is a hypothesis and not a settled view.

The number of temples is disputed. Bárta's account gives six sun temples in the dynasty [@archaeology-sun-kings-2020, six-temples paragraph]. Magli notes that texts of the period suggest Sahure, Neferefre, Neferirkare and Menkauhor also built them, but these temples have never been found. Some scholars (citing Verner 2002 and Nuzzolo 2007) hold that those texts refer to renewals of Userkaf's temple, so that Niuserre's was the only other temple actually built. Magli himself argues that the missing temples never existed [@magli-2009, PDF pp. 10–11]. The firm archaeological evidence is therefore for two temples, Userkaf's and Niuserre's. Dates for both are approximate.

ideas.title: The Alphabet

date.marks: The earliest known alphabetic inscriptions, from Egypt and Sinai
date.note: The earliest alphabetic inscriptions lack stratified archaeological contexts, so their dates are uncertain [@lam-2010, p. 189]. The 22-letter alphabet associated with the Phoenicians stabilized around 1000 BCE [@lam-2010, p. 192].

ideas.origin: Semitic-speaking workers in Egypt and Sinai; later standardized by the Phoenicians
ideas.summary: Semitic speakers in Egypt borrow hieroglyphic pictures but use each one for a single sound. A few dozen signs can write a whole language. Most of the world's major scripts, from Latin and Cyrillic to Arabic and Devanagari, descend from it.
ideas.body:
**Invention.** The earliest alphabetic inscriptions come from Serabit el-Khadem, an Egyptian mining site in Sinai, and from Wadi el-Hol near Thebes [@lam-2010, p. 189]. The two Wadi el-Hol inscriptions date to roughly 1900–1800 BCE [@herrmann-2023]. "The alphabet was invented among Semitic speakers in the Egyptian realm, inspired iconographically by hieroglyphic writing but not bound by its modes of expression" [@lam-2010, p. 190]. Workers at the Sinai turquoise mines, or Canaanites living in Egypt, are the likeliest inventors [@herrmann-2023].

**How it worked.** Each sign took its sound from the first consonant of the West Semitic word for the thing pictured (the *acrophonic principle*): a hand, *kaph*, stood for /k/ [@lam-2010, pp. 189–190]. Alphabets need tens of signs where logographic and syllabic systems need hundreds. Most of the world's common languages, Chinese and Japanese aside, are written in scripts descended from this linear West Semitic alphabet [@lam-2010, p. 189].

**Development.** Proto-Canaanite inscriptions in the Levant run from the 17th century BCE, and most date from the 13th century or later. Around 1000 BCE the script stabilized as a 22-letter alphabet written right to left, matching the sounds of Phoenician. Hebrew and Aramaic speakers adopted it, and the oldest Greek inscriptions appear in the 8th century BCE [@lam-2010, pp. 191–193].

**A caution about literacy.** It is tempting to say the alphabet put literacy within everyone's reach. Lam argues against this: although it probably made scribal training easier, "no immediate correlation can be made between alphabetic writing and broad literacy" [@lam-2010, p. 189].

ideas.title: Buddhism

date.marks: The death of the Buddha; his teaching career came in the decades before
date.note: Traditional Theravada chronology puts his death in 544/543 BCE; a corrected version gives 487/486 BCE, and the Indian "short chronology" 370–368 BCE [@violatti-2015]. A review of the 1988 Göttingen symposium on the question favoured about 400 BCE [@cousins-1996].

ideas.origin: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha; northern India
ideas.summary: In his first sermon, near Varanasi, the Buddha sets out the Four Noble Truths: suffering arises from craving, and it ends when craving is let go.
ideas.body:
**The teaching.** The Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, traditionally the Buddha's first sermon, delivered at Isipatana near Varanasi, identifies the origin of suffering as "the craving that makes for further becoming" and its cessation as "the remainderless fading & cessation, renunciation, relinquishment, release, & letting go of that very craving" [@sn-56-11].

**The dating problem.** The Theravada tradition dates the Buddha's death to 544/543 BCE. Checking it against the reign of the emperor Ashoka produced a corrected date of 487/486 BCE, while Indian sources point to 370–368 BCE. At a 1988 symposium on the question in Göttingen, experts proposed dates ranging from 486 to 261 BCE [@violatti-2015]. Reviewing the published volumes, Cousins concluded that "the evidence seems to favour some kind of median chronology and we should no doubt speak of a date for the Buddha's Mahaparinibbana of c.400 B.C." [@cousins-1996].

ideas.title: The Examined Life
ideas.summary: Truth is pursued by relentless questioning. Executed for it, Socrates makes intellectual inquiry a moral act.

ideas.title: Formal Logic
ideas.summary: The syllogism codifies valid reasoning itself. Aristotle's system would dominate Western and Islamic thought for 2,000 years.

ideas.title: Axiomatic Proof
ideas.summary: From a handful of axioms, all of geometry follows by proof. The template for rigorous knowledge ever since.

ideas.title: Christianity
ideas.summary: A message of universal love and salvation that would become the faith of the Roman Empire and reshape the West.

ideas.title: Paper
ideas.summary: A cheap, light writing surface from plant fibre. It travels the Silk Road and makes books abundant.

ideas.title: Mathematical Astronomy
ideas.summary: An Earth-centred cosmos described with geometric precision — wrong, but predictive enough to reign for 1,400 years.

ideas.title: Islam
ideas.summary: A unifying faith and legal tradition that, within a century, spans from Spain to Central Asia.

ideas.title: Zero as a Number
ideas.summary: Zero gets rules of arithmetic of its own. With Hindu–Arabic numerals, calculation becomes something anyone can do.

ideas.title: Algebra
ideas.summary: Systematic methods for solving equations. His name gives us the word algorithm.

ideas.title: The University
ideas.summary: A self-governing community of scholars. Learning gains an institution independent of monastery and court.

ideas.title: Rule of Law
ideas.summary: Even the king is bound by law. A narrow baronial deal becomes a lasting symbol of limits on power.

ideas.title: The Printing Press
ideas.summary: Movable metal type makes books cheap and identical. Within fifty years, millions are in circulation.

ideas.title: Political Realism
ideas.summary: Politics described as it is, not as it ought to be. Power is analysed on its own terms.

ideas.title: The Reformation
ideas.summary: Individual conscience and scripture over Church authority. Printing spreads the challenge across Europe in weeks.

ideas.title: Heliocentrism
ideas.summary: The Earth moves around the Sun. Humanity is displaced from the centre of the cosmos.

ideas.title: The Scientific Method
ideas.summary: Knowledge built from systematic observation and experiment rather than inherited authority.

ideas.title: Universal Laws of Nature
ideas.summary: The same mathematical laws govern a falling apple and orbiting planets. The universe becomes a knowable machine.

ideas.title: Natural Rights
ideas.summary: People are born with rights to life, liberty and property; government is legitimate only by their consent.

ideas.title: Separation of Powers
ideas.origin: Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws
ideas.summary: Liberty is safest when legislative, executive and judicial power check one another.

ideas.title: The Market Economy
ideas.origin: Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations
ideas.summary: Self-interest, coordinated by markets and the division of labour, produces collective prosperity.

ideas.title: Universal Rights
ideas.origin: Declaration of the Rights of Man, France
ideas.summary: Rights belong to all people by nature. Revolutions in America and France put Enlightenment ideas into practice.

ideas.title: Women's Rights
ideas.summary: If rights are universal, they belong to women too. An argument that would take centuries to win.

ideas.title: Historical Materialism
ideas.summary: History is a struggle between classes; capitalism will give way to collective ownership. It would move nations.

ideas.title: Evolution by Natural Selection
ideas.origin: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species
ideas.summary: All life descends from common ancestors, shaped by selection over immense time. Humanity joins the animal kingdom.

ideas.title: Individual Liberty
ideas.summary: The only justification for restricting a person's freedom is to prevent harm to others.

ideas.title: Germ Theory

date.marks: Pasteur's campaign against spontaneous generation begins
date.note: Germ theory took shape over several decades rather than at one moment. Key work runs from Semmelweis (1847) to Koch's anthrax paper (1876) and beyond [@cavaillon-2022; @blevins-2010].

ideas.origin: Semmelweis, Pasteur, Davaine, Lister, Koch and others
ideas.summary: Specific diseases are caused by specific living microorganisms. Built up over decades of experiments by many researchers, the idea made antiseptic surgery possible and launched medical bacteriology.
ideas.body:
**Many hands.** Precursors of germ theory go back at least to Girolamo Fracastoro (1546), who thought diseases spread through "seminaria," or seeds [@cavaillon-2022]. The theory's 19th-century foundations were laid by several people:

- **Semmelweis (1847)** showed that medical students' hands, after autopsies, carried infection to women giving birth [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Pasteur (from 1860–61)** took up the Academy of Sciences' challenge to settle the question of spontaneous generation. The decisive swan-neck flask experiments, which showed that the air carries germs, were conceived by his colleague Antoine Balard [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Davaine (1863)** found bacteria in the blood of animals with anthrax and showed that the disease spread through infected blood. Historians credit him with the first demonstration that a bacterium causes disease [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Lister (1865)** learned of Pasteur's theory and applied it to surgery, using phenol as an antiseptic [@cavaillon-2022].
- **Koch (1876)** published his study of the anthrax bacillus [@koch-1876]. This work "launched the field of medical bacteriology" [@blevins-2010].

**Myth and reality.** Cavaillon and Legout write explicitly to separate Pasteur's real achievements from "the legend built by his hagiographers," in part a legend he cultivated himself [@cavaillon-2022]. Crediting the theory to one or two famous names misrepresents how it was built.

ideas.title: The Unconscious Mind
ideas.origin: Sigmund Freud, The Interpretation of Dreams
ideas.summary: Much of what drives us is hidden from ourselves. The self is no longer fully transparent to reason.

ideas.title: Relativity
ideas.summary: Space and time are not absolute but bend with motion and gravity. Mass and energy are interchangeable.

ideas.title: Quantum Mechanics
ideas.summary: At the smallest scales, nature is probabilistic. The clockwork universe gives way to uncertainty.

ideas.title: Universal Computation
ideas.summary: A single abstract machine can perform any computation. The theoretical blueprint for every computer.

ideas.title: Universal Human Rights
ideas.summary: After world war and genocide, the nations of the world affirm rights belonging to every human being.

ideas.title: Information Theory
ideas.summary: Information can be measured in bits and transmitted reliably through noise. The foundation of digital communication.

ideas.title: The Double Helix
ideas.summary: Heredity is written in a molecular code. Life itself becomes legible as information.

ideas.title: Paradigm Shifts
ideas.summary: Science advances not steadily but through revolutions that overturn whole frameworks of thought.

ideas.title: Packet-Switched Networks
ideas.summary: Computers talk to each other by breaking messages into packets. The seed of the internet.

ideas.title: The World Wide Web
ideas.summary: Hyperlinked documents open to anyone. Publishing becomes nearly free, as printing once made copying cheap.

ideas.title: Deep Learning
ideas.summary: Neural networks trained on vast data surpass hand-built systems. Machines learn from examples, not rules.

ideas.title: The Transformer

date.marks: Publication of "Attention Is All You Need"

ideas.origin: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need"
ideas.summary: A neural network architecture built on attention alone, without recurrence, so it can be trained efficiently in parallel. It became the basis of language models such as BERT (2018) and GPT-3 (2020).
ideas.body:
**The idea.** The paper proposed "a new simple network architecture, the Transformer, based solely on attention mechanisms, dispensing with recurrence and convolutions entirely." The authors reported that it was "more parallelizable" and required "significantly less time to train" than the recurrent and convolutional models it replaced [@vaswani-2017, abstract].

**What was new.** Attention itself was older. It had already been added to recurrent translation models, letting a model "(soft-)search for parts of a source sentence that are relevant to predicting a target word" [@bahdanau-2014, abstract]. The Transformer's step was to make attention the whole architecture.

**What followed.** BERT, short for "Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers" [@devlin-2018, abstract], was built on it. So was GPT-3, which uses "the same model and architecture as GPT-2" with sparse attention patterns "in the layers of the transformer" [@brown-2020, §2.1].

date.marks: Midpoint of 'approximately 1.2–1.1 Myr' from palaeomagnetism, cosmogenic nuclides and biostratigraphy.

events.summary: A human mandible with Mode 1 stone tools and cut-marked fauna was deposited in level TE9 of Sima del Elefante, dated to approximately 1.2–1.1 million years ago.
events.body:
> a human mandible associated with an assemblage of Mode 1 lithic tools and faunal remains bearing traces of hominin processing, in stratigraphic level TE9 [@carbonell-2008, Abstract]

> Level TE9 has been dated to the Early Pleistocene (approximately 1.2–1.1 Myr) [@carbonell-2008, Abstract]

events.title: Kocabaş skull, Denizli Basin

date.marks: Midpoint of '1.2–1.1 Ma' as cited secondhand in Despriée et al. 2024.
date.note: Cited secondhand; the original dating study was not read.

events.summary: The Kocabaş skull is dated to 1.2–1.1 Ma, cited as suggesting hominin passages through Anatolia.
events.body: > the discovery of the Kocabas skull (1.2–1.1 Ma), suggest possible hominin passages [@despriee-2024, Introduction]

events.title: Core-and-flake occupation at Pont-de-Lavaud, Creuse valley

date.marks: Weighted average ESR age of 1054 ± 54 ka as reported in the Lunery paper.

events.summary: A core-and-flake assemblage at Pont-de-Lavaud in the Creuse valley is dated by ESR to about 1 Ma, with weighted average ages of 1054 ± 54 ka.
events.body: > a core and flake assemblage dated to c.a 1 Ma, with weighted average ages of 1054 ± 54 ka [@despriee-2024, Introduction]

events.title: Stone artefacts deposited at Calio, Sulawesi

date.marks: Minimum age of 1.04 Ma by palaeomagnetic dating and coupled U-series/ESR dating of fossil teeth; possibly up to 1.48 Ma.
date.note: Source gives a minimum age of 1.04 Ma with a possible upper range to 1.48 Ma.

events.summary: Stone artefacts occur at Calio in fossiliferous layers dated to at least 1.04 Ma and possibly up to 1.48 Ma, indicating hominins on Sulawesi.
events.body:
> stone artefacts also occur at the nearby site of Calio in fossiliferous layers dated to at least 1.04 Ma and possibly up to 1.48 Ma [@hakim-2025, Abstract]

> Sulawesi was populated by hominins at around the same time as Flores, if not earlier [@hakim-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Flaked stone artefacts deposited at Wolo Sege, Flores

date.marks: Minimum age 1.02 ± 0.02 Ma as cited in Hakim et al. 2025.

events.summary: Flaked stone artefacts were deposited at Wolo Sege on Flores at least 1.02 ± 0.02 million years ago, the earlier oldest indication of hominins in Wallacea.
events.body: > flaked stone artefacts deposited at least 1.02 ± 0.02 million years ago (Ma) at Wolo Sege on Flores [@hakim-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Burning in Wonderwerk Cave during early Acheulean occupation

date.marks: Approximately 1.0 Ma, as given by the authors for the early Acheulean occupation.

events.place: Wonderwerk Cave, Northern Cape, South Africa
events.summary: Burned bone and ashed plant remains in stratum 10 show burning took place in the cave during the early Acheulean occupation, approximately 1.0 Ma.
events.body:
> burning took place in the cave during the early Acheulean occupation, approximately 1.0 Ma [@berna-2012, Abstract]

> in the form of burned bone and ashed plant remains [@berna-2012, Abstract]

events.title: Homo erectus calvaria and early Acheulean tools at Daka, Bouri

date.marks: About 1.0 Myr, the age given for the Dakanihylo Member sediments.

events.summary: A hominin calvaria and postcranial remains from the Dakanihylo Member of the Bouri Formation lie in sediments about 1.0 million years old that contain abundant early Acheulean tools.
events.body:
> A hominid calvaria and postcranial remains recently recovered from the Dakanihylo Member of the Bouri Formation, Middle Awash, Ethiopia [@asfaw-2002, Abstract]

> ∼1.0-million-year (Myr)-old Pleistocene sediments contain abundant early Acheulean stone tools [@asfaw-2002, Abstract]

events.title: Homo erectus-like cranium UA 31 deposited at Buia, Eritrea

date.marks: Aalat deposits 'well-constrained around 1 Ma' by magnetostratigraphy and radiometric records.

events.place: Buia, Dandiero basin, Danakil depression, Eritrea
events.summary: A Homo erectus-like cranium (UA 31) from the Aalat deposits of the Danakil depression is dated to about 1 million years, within the Jaramillo subchron interval.
events.body:
> The Homo erectus-like cranium from Buia (UA 31) was [@bruner-2016, Abstract]

> found in the Eritrean Danakil depression and dated to 1 million years [@bruner-2016, Abstract]

events.title: Large cutting tools deposited at Barranc de la Boella

date.marks: About 1 million years ago, from palaeomagnetic and cosmogenic-nuclide dating reported by the excavators.

events.place: Barranc de la Boella, la Canonja, Spain
events.summary: A lithic assemblage including large cutting tools was deposited at Barranc de la Boella near Tarragona, dated by the excavators to about 1 million years ago.
aliases: Barranc de la Boella Acheulian assemblage
events.body:
> the Barranc de la Boella site which has yielded a lithic assemblage dating to [@vallverdu-2014, Abstract]

> ∼1 million years ago that includes large cutting tools (LCT) [@vallverdu-2014, Abstract]

events.title: Flint artefacts at Happisburgh Site 3

date.marks: Source gives 'ca. 850 ky or possibly ca. 950 ky' from the Early Pleistocene Cromer Forest-bed sequence; placement year is the midpoint of the two alternatives.
date.note: The source gives two alternative ages (about 850 ka or about 950 ka).

events.summary: Humanly made flint flakes, flake tools and cores were recovered from lag gravels at Happisburgh Site 3, dated to about 850,000 or possibly 950,000 years ago.
events.body:
> dating to ca. 850 ky or possibly ca. 950 ky [@ashton-2014, Methods and Analysis]

> An artefact assemblage has been recovered from these lag gravels, consisting of flint flakes, flake tools and cores. [@ashton-2014, Methods and Analysis]

events.title: Hominin footprint surface formed in estuarine silts at Happisburgh

date.marks: Midpoint of the source's stratigraphic range 'between ca. 1 million and 0.78 million years ago' for the Hill House Formation; the footprints themselves were exposed in May 2013.
date.note: The sediments are bracketed only by stratigraphy to roughly 1 to 0.78 million years ago; the placement year is the midpoint, not a measured age.

events.summary: A surface of elongated hollows interpreted as hominin footprints, in estuarine silts dated to between about 1 and 0.78 million years ago, was exposed on the Happisburgh foreshore in 2013.
events.body:
> oldest known hominin footprint surface outside Africa at between ca. 1 million and 0.78 million years ago [@ashton-2014, Abstract]

> the hollows are distinctly elongated and the majority fall within the range of juvenile to adult hominin foot sizes [@ashton-2014, Abstract]

> In May 2013 extensive areas of the laminated sediments were exposed on the foreshore. [@ashton-2014, Abstract]

events.title: Cut-marked Homo antecessor remains at Gran Dolina TD6

date.marks: 850,000 years ago, as given by the excavating team in 2025.

events.place: Gran Dolina, Sierra de Atapuerca, Spain
events.summary: Human remains from level TD6 attributed to Homo antecessor, including a child's cervical vertebra with cut marks, are dated by the excavators to 850,000 years ago.
events.body:
> A human cervical vertebra, dated to 850,000 years ago, shows clear cut marks consistent with intentional decapitation. [@iphes-2025, news item]

> All are attributed to the species Homo antecessor [@iphes-2025, news item]

events.title: Homo antecessor remains accumulate in Gran Dolina TD6, Atapuerca

date.marks: Layer dated 'between 950 ka and 770 ka' per a 2026 summary; year placed at the start of the requested period because the range extends beyond it.
date.note: The dating range is wide and straddles the start of the period.

events.place: Gran Dolina, Sierra de Atapuerca (Burgos, Spain)
events.summary: The TD6 unit at Gran Dolina yielded around 170 Homo antecessor bones; the layer is dated between about 950 and 770 ka.
events.body:
> The Homo antecessor fossils from the TD6 layer of Gran Dolina at Atapuerca, Spain, dated between 950 ka and 770 ka [@hublin-2026, Abstract]

> whose records include around 170 hominin bones that have allowed the definition of a new species, Homo antecessor. [@campana-2016, Abstract]

events.title: Large cutting tools deposited in tektite layer, Bose Basin, China

date.marks: Date of the tektite layer in which the tools occurred, given as 803,000 ± 3,000 years (per Hou et al. 2000 as summarised by the Smithsonian); year placed at the young end of that range to fall within the period.
date.note: Later Ar-Ar work places the Australasian tektite-forming impact itself nearer 788–785 ka, so the Bose layer date has been debated.

events.summary: Handaxe-like large cutting tools were excavated in the Bose Basin solely within a tektite layer dated to about 803,000 years ago, together with charred wood.
events.body:
> The tools occurred solely in the tektite layer – a stroke of luck in that the tektites can be dated accurately – to 803,000 + 3,000 years. [@smithsonian-bose, Bose, China]

> our team found the oldest known large cutting tools in China, which resemble the handaxes of their African contemporaries in several ways. [@smithsonian-bose, Bose, China]

events.title: Australasian tektite-forming meteorite impact

date.marks: c. 788 to 785 ka, as stated in the source abstract.
date.note: Other studies date the tektite layer at Bose to about 803 ka; estimates differ by method.

events.place: Mainland South-East Asia (impact site not conclusively located)
events.summary: A large meteorite impact in mainland South-East Asia produced the Australasian tektite strewn field, dated to about 788–785 ka; the crater has not been located conclusively.
events.body:
> The MIS 20 large meteorite impact ( c ., 788 to 785 ka) occurred within mainland South-East Asia [@carling-2024, Abstract]

> The importance of the questions raised relate to the search for the impact site, which has not been located conclusively. [@carling-2024, Abstract]

events.title: Fish cooked on site at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov

date.marks: About 0.78 million years ago (MIS 18–20) as given in the source.

events.place: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (paleo-Lake Hula margin, Israel)
events.summary: Taphonomic and X-ray diffraction study of fish remains in Layer II-6 argues that hominins cooked and ate large cyprinid fish beside hearths at the site about 0.78 million years ago.
aliases: Evidence for the cooking of fish at GBY
events.body:
> suggesting, together with the archaeological and taphonomic data, that the fish from the archaeological horizons of Area B had been cooked and consumed on site. [@zohar-2022, Abstract]

> This is the earliest evidence of cooking by hominins. [@zohar-2022, Abstract]

events.title: Hominins make hearths at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, Israel

date.marks: About 0.78 million years ago (~0.78 Ma, MIS 18–20; layers above the Matuyama–Brunhes boundary), as stated by the excavators' publications.
date.note: The site's sequence spans some 100 ka (MIS 20–18); individual hearth horizons fall within that span.

events.place: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (paleo-Lake Hula margin, Israel)
events.summary: Acheulian hominins occupying the paleo-Lake Hula shore at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov left 'latent' hearths, identified through clusters of burned flint microartifacts, in occupation horizons of about 0.78 million years ago.
events.body:
> The early Middle Pleistocene site of Gesher Benot Ya’aqov, Israel (marine isotope stages 18–20; ~0.78 million years ago), has preserved evidence of hearth-related hominin activities [@zohar-2022, Abstract]

> Research at the Acheulian site of Gesher Benot Ya‘aqov (GBY) has revealed the presence of latent hearths, identifiable only through spatial analysis of burned and unburned flint microartifacts [@alperson-afil-2017, Introduction]

events.title: Starch-rich plants processed with percussive tools at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov

date.marks: 'At least 780,000 y ago' per the source; occupations assigned to MIS 18–20.

events.place: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov (paleo-Lake Hula margin, Israel)
events.summary: Starch grains on basalt anvils and percussors from two occupation levels show hominins at Gesher Benot Ya'aqov processed acorns, grass grains, water plants and legumes at least 780,000 years ago.
events.body: > a wide variety of plants were processed by Middle Pleistocene hominins at the site of Gesher Benot Ya’aqov in Israel, at least 780,000 y ago. [@ahituv-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Hominins living at Grotte à Hominidés, Thomas Quarry I, Casablanca

date.marks: Around 773 ka, from magnetostratigraphy placing the remains close to the Matuyama–Brunhes transition, with biochronological agreement.

events.summary: Hominin mandibles, teeth and vertebrae from the Grotte à Hominidés at Thomas Quarry I are dated to around 773 ka and are morphologically distinct from Homo antecessor.
events.body: > new hominin fossils from the Grotte à Hominidés at Thomas Quarry I (ThI-GH) in Casablanca, Morocco, dated to around 773 ka. [@hublin-2026, Abstract]

events.title: Matuyama–Brunhes geomagnetic reversal

date.marks: ~773 ka for the final reversal, from 40Ar/39Ar dates on lavas tied to astronomically dated sediments.

events.place: Global (dated in lava flows, sediments and ice cores)
events.summary: Earth's last magnetic polarity reversal, with field weakening from about 795 ka, an excursion at about 784 ka, and a final polarity flip at about 773 ka.
events.body:
> The final 180° polarity reversal at ~773 ka culminates a complex process beginning at ~795 ka with weakening of the field [@singer-2019, Abstract]

> Earth’s last magnetic field reversal was complex, with excursions at 795 and 784 ka before a final polarity flip at 773 ka. [@singer-2019, Abstract]

events.title: Bishop Tuff eruption forms Long Valley Caldera

date.marks: 767 ka as given in the USGS field guide.

events.summary: The caldera-forming Bishop Tuff eruption at Long Valley evacuated about 650 cubic km of rhyolite magma in 5–6 days, about 767 ka.
events.body: > The Bishop Tuff, pyroclastic product of the 767-ka caldera-forming eruption at Long Valley, represents evacuation of ~650 km3 of rhyolite magma from a unitary zoned chamber in 5–6 days. [@hildreth-2017, A Refreshing Overview of the Bishop Tuff, Abstract]

events.title: Small-bodied hominins at Mata Menge, Flores

date.marks: About 0.7 Ma (40Ar/39Ar, fission-track and U-series/ESR dating); placed just inside the period boundary.
date.note: The source gives 'around 700 thousand years ago', which falls at the end boundary of the period.

events.summary: A mandible fragment and six teeth of at least three small-jawed individuals, with simple stone tools, were deposited at Mata Menge about 700,000 years ago; they resemble Homo floresiensis.
events.body:
> Dating to ~0.7 Ma, these fossils now constitute the oldest hominin remains from Flores [@vandenbergh-2016, Abstract]

> deposited in a small valley stream around 700 thousand years ago [@brumm-2016, Abstract]

events.title: Butchered rhinoceros and stone tools at Kalinga, Luzon

date.marks: Placement year is a round figure within the 777–631 ka bone-bed range obtained by electron-spin resonance on tooth enamel and fluvial quartz
date.note: The source gives a range of 777–631 ka rather than a single date; the placement year is a round figure within the range, not a point estimate.

events.summary: A bone bed at Kalinga yielded 57 stone tools with a butchered Rhinoceros philippinensis skeleton, dated by ESR to between 777 and 631 thousand years ago.
events.body:
> Kalinga in the Cagayan Valley of northern Luzon in the Philippines that have yielded 57 stone tools associated with an almost-complete disarticulated skeleton of Rhinoceros philippinensis , which shows clear signs of butchery [@ingicco-2018, Abstract]

> dated to between 777 and 631 thousand years ago using electron-spin resonance methods that were applied to tooth enamel and fluvial quartz [@ingicco-2018, Abstract]

events.title: Flint artefacts deposited at Pakefield, Suffolk

date.marks: About 700 kyr ago, from lithostratigraphy, palaeomagnetism, amino acid geochronology and biostratigraphy

events.summary: Flint artefacts in the Cromer Forest-bed Formation at Pakefield are dated to about 700 ka, interpreted by the authors as evidence for human presence in northern Europe.
events.body:
> flint artefacts from the Cromer Forest-bed Formation at Pakefield (52° N), Suffolk, UK [@parfitt-2005, Abstract]

> the artefacts date to the early part of the Brunhes Chron (about 700 kyr ago) [@parfitt-2005, Abstract]

events.title: Hominins at Mata Menge, Flores, in a stream deposit

date.marks: About 700 thousand years ago, from 40Ar/39Ar and fission-track dates on bracketing volcanic deposits plus coupled U-series/ESR dating of fossil teeth

events.summary: A fluvial sandstone layer at Mata Menge, which yielded in situ hominin fossils attributed to a population ancestral to Homo floresiensis, was deposited around 700 ka.
events.body:
> The fluvial sandstone layer from which the in situ fossils were excavated in 2014 was deposited in a small valley stream around 700 thousand years ago [@brumm-2016, Abstract]

> Recent excavations at the early Middle Pleistocene site of Mata Menge in the So’a Basin of central Flores, Indonesia [@brumm-2016, Abstract]

> attributed to a population ancestral to Late Pleistocene Homo floresiensis [@brumm-2016, Abstract]

events.title: Earliest suggested hominin occupation at Old Park, Canterbury

date.marks: Placement year is a rough point within the 773-607 ka range for the earliest artefact-bearing sediment; occupation is inferred, not directly dated
date.note: The range is broad (773-607 ka); the placement year is a rough point within it and the occupation is described as only suggested.

events.place: Old Park (Fordwich Pit), Canterbury, Kent (United Kingdom)
events.summary: Radiometric and palaeomagnetic dating places the earliest suggested occupation of Old Park between 773 and 607 ka, with hominin presence inferred during MIS 17-16.
events.body: > Radiometric and palaeomagnetic dating places the earliest suggested occupation of this site between 773 thousand years ago (ka) and 607 ka, with hominin presence inferred during MIS 17–16. [@key-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Early Acheulean occupations at Notarchirico, Basilicata

date.marks: Midpoint of the 695-670 ka range from 40Ar/39Ar on tephras and ESR on bleached quartz
date.note: Placement is the midpoint of the published 695-670 ka range.

events.summary: Four older occupation levels at Notarchirico, one with bifaces, are dated by 40Ar/39Ar and ESR to between 695 and 670 ka (MIS 17).
events.body:
> four older occupation levels have recently been unearthed, including one with bifaces [@moncel-2020, Abstract]

> place these occupations between 695 and 670 ka (MIS 17) [@moncel-2020, Abstract]

events.title: Acheulean occupation at La Noira, Centre France

date.marks: ESR weighted average of 665±55 ka on fluvial sands overlying the archaeological level (a minimum age for the occupation)
date.note: The ESR age is for the overlying sands; the authors present the occupation as about 700 ka old.

events.summary: An Acheulean assemblage with large cutting tools at La Noira lies under fluvial sands ESR-dated to 665±55 ka, so the occupation is older than that.
events.body:
> the weighted average age obtained for the fluvial sands overlying the slope deposits is 665±55 ka [@moncel-2013, Abstract]

> The lithic series is classified as Acheulean on the basis of both technological and typological analyses. [@moncel-2013, Abstract]

> At la Noira (Brinay, Central France) [@moncel-2013, Abstract]

events.title: Acheulian occupation at Moulin Quignon, Somme valley

date.marks: Midpoint of 670-650 ka, dated by ESR on quartz to early MIS 16

events.summary: Fluvial deposits at Moulin Quignon yielded over 260 flint artefacts including five bifaces, ESR-dated to early MIS 16, about 670-650 ka.
events.body:
> the first Acheulian occupation north of 50°N occurred around 670–650 ka ago [@antoine-2019, Abstract]

> More than 260 flint artefacts were recovered, including large flakes, cores and five bifaces. [@antoine-2019, Abstract]

events.title: Homo erectus remains at Chenjiawo, Lantian

date.marks: About 0.65 Myr, from paleomagnetic polarity determinations and lithostratigraphic position in the loess-paleosol sequence (1989 study)
date.note: The 1989 magnetostratigraphic estimate; later studies may differ.

events.summary: Homo erectus remains at the Chenjiawo locality near Lantian in middle Pleistocene loess are dated about 0.65 Myr old by paleomagnetic polarity and loess-paleosol position.
events.body:
> whereas the remains found at the Chenjiawo locality in middle Pleistocene loess are about 0.65 myr old [@an-1989, Abstract]

> Skeletal remains of Homo erectus found in Pleistocene loess at two sites near Lantian in central China [@an-1989, Abstract]

events.title: Eruption of the Lava Creek Tuff forms Yellowstone Caldera

date.marks: About 631,000 years ago as stated by the USGS Yellowstone Volcano Observatory (geochronology of the volcanic rocks)

events.summary: The Lava Creek Tuff eruption evacuated much of the magma reservoir and formed Yellowstone Caldera by ground collapse, about 631,000 years ago.
events.body: > 631,000 years ago: Eruption of the Lava Creek Tuff evacuated much of the magma reservoir and formed Yellowstone Caldera as the overlying ground surface collapsed. [@stelten-2022, main text]

events.title: Bodo cranium individual in the Middle Awash, Ethiopia

date.marks: Age of about 600,000 years as stated by the source; the dating method is not given in the excerpt
date.note: The cranium was found in 1976. The age is a rounded figure.

events.summary: The Bodo cranium from the Middle Awash of Ethiopia is described as about 600,000 years old, an early Middle Pleistocene hominid skull assigned by some authors to Homo heidelbergensis.
events.body: > The 600,000-year-old cranium from Bodo, Ethiopia, is the oldest and most complete early Middle Pleistocene hominid skull from Africa. [@conroy-2000, Abstract]

events.title: Hominin tooth and tools deposited at Isernia La Pineta, Italy

date.marks: Midpoint of the 40Ar/39Ar age range of about 583–561 ka given for archaeological level 3 coll (end of MIS 15)
date.note: The tooth was excavated in 2014; the date is that of the dated deposit, not of the find.

events.summary: A human deciduous incisor (IS42) was found in level 3 coll at Isernia La Pineta with a handaxe-free flake industry; 40Ar/39Ar dating places the level at about 583–561 ka, the end of MIS 15.
events.body:
> An isolated human deciduous incisor (labelled IS42) was discovered in 2014 within the archaeological level 3 coll (overlying layer 3a) that, according to new 40 Ar/ 39 Ar measurements, is dated to about 583–561 ka [@peretto-2015, Abstract]

> characterized by the absence of handaxes and reduction strategies primarily aimed at the production of small/medium-sized flakes [@peretto-2015, Abstract]

events.title: Artefact-bearing gravels deposited at Fordwich Pit, Kent

date.marks: Midpoint of IR-RF (feldspar) minimum ages 570 ± 36 and 513 ± 30 ka; MIS 15 artefact production approx. 560–620 ka
date.note: The IR-RF ages are minimum ages for the artefacts; the 330+ handaxes found in the 1920s are suggested to be of similar MIS 15 age, while some excavated artefacts come from levels dated 347–385 ka.

events.place: Fordwich Pit, Old Park (Canterbury, Kent, UK)
events.summary: Excavated flakes, scrapers and cores at Fordwich come from levels with IR-RF minimum ages of 570 ± 36 to 513 ± 30 ka, assigned most plausibly to MIS 14 deposition, with artefacts made during MIS 15.
events.body:
> Infrared-radiofluorescence (IR-RF) dating of feldspar reveals 112 artefacts to have come from levels dating to at least 570 ± 36 to 513 ± 30 thousand years ago (ka) [@key-2022, Abstract]

> most plausibly assigned to an MIS 14 deposition, with artefacts produced during MIS 15 (approx. 560–620 ka) [@key-2022, Abstract]

events.title: Blade and blade-core production in the Kapthurin Formation, Kenya

date.marks: At least 509 ± 9 ka, as reported by Johnson and McBrearty (2010) and cited by Wilkins and Chazan (2012)
date.note: A minimum age; another passage in the same paper gives the Kapthurin blade assemblages as 550–500 ka.

events.summary: Blades and blade cores occur in the Kapthurin Formation of the Kenya Rift Valley, dated to at least 509 ± 9 ka.
events.body:
> In East Africa, the earliest occurrence of blades and blade cores date to at least 509 ± 9 ka in the Kapthurin Formation (Johnson and McBrearty, 2010). [@wilkins-2012, Introduction]

> the Kapthurin Formation, Kenya 550–500 ka [@wilkins-2012, Conclusions]

events.title: Hominins at Thomas Quarry I Hominid Cave, Casablanca, Morocco

date.marks: US/ESR age of 501 +94/−76 ka on a human premolar (laser ablation ICP-MS)
date.note: Dating is disputed: OSL of embedding sediments indicates about 400 ka, while biochronology and lithostratigraphy point to greater antiquity, near the base of the Middle Pleistocene. Most of the US/ESR range falls before 500 ka.

events.place: Thomas Quarry I, Grotte à Hominidés (Casablanca, Morocco)
events.summary: Unit 4 of the Hominid Cave holds hominin fossils with Acheulean artefacts and fauna; a human premolar gives a US/ESR age of 501 +94/−76 ka, though OSL on the sediments gives about 400 ka.
events.body:
> has given a US/ESR age of 501 +94 76 ka for a human premolar, while OSL measurements indicate an age of circa 400 ky for embedding sediments. [@daujeard-2016, Site Description: Stratigraphy and age]

> biochronological and lithostratigraphic evidence point to a greater antiquity, closer to the base of the Middle Pleistocene [@daujeard-2016, Site Description: Stratigraphy and age]

> was associated with Acheulean artefacts and a rich mammalian fauna [@daujeard-2016, Abstract]

events.title: Middle Toba Tuff eruption, Toba caldera, Sumatra

date.marks: Age of 501 ka for the Middle Toba Tuff as cited by Reid and Vazquez (2017)

events.summary: The Middle Toba Tuff erupted from the Toba Caldera Complex about 501 ka, the penultimate caldera-related eruption before the 74 ka Youngest Toba Tuff.
events.body:
> YTT: 74 ka Youngest Toba Tuff; MTT: 501 ka Middle Toba Tuff [@reid-2017, Fig. 1 caption]

> before the penultimate caldera-related eruption at 501 ka [@reid-2017, Abstract]

events.title: Elephant-bone knapping tool used at Boxgrove

date.marks: '~480,000-year-old Acheulean context'; sequence dated by biostratigraphy to the MIS 13/12 transition

events.summary: A cortical bone fragment from an elephant was deliberately shaped and used as a percussor to resharpen flint tools in an Acheulean context at Boxgrove.
events.body: > a knapping tool made on an elephant bone from a ~480,000-year-old Acheulean context at Boxgrove, UK [@parfitt-2026, Introduction]

events.title: Hominins butcher a horse at Boxgrove Horse Butchery Site

date.marks: 'Some 480,000 years ago' as given by the excavator; the deposits correlate to the MIS 13/12 transition (biostratigraphy)
date.note: The Boxgrove sequence is dated mainly by mammalian biostratigraphy, with MIS 13 (533-478 ka) marine deposits overlain by MIS 12 terrestrial sediments.

events.summary: At the Horse Butchery Site a large horse was slaughtered and processed, with flint handaxe manufacture, by Homo heidelbergensis; tide-laid silts then sealed the site.
events.body:
> a spot where a large horse was slaughtered and processed some 480,000 years ago [@pope-2020, paras 2-3]

> fossils of Homo heidelbergensis [@pope-2020, para 1]

events.title: Soft hammers of antler and bone used in knapping at Boxgrove

date.marks: 'dating to ~480,000 years ago' per the authors

events.summary: Modified antlers and large mammal bones were used as soft hammers alongside flint hard hammers to make finely worked ovate handaxes of the Boxgrove Acheulean.
events.body: > The earliest known soft hammers, dating to ~480,000 years ago, come from Boxgrove (UK), where modified antlers and large mammal bones were used alongside flint hard hammers. [@parfitt-2026, Abstract]

events.title: Fauresmith assemblage with blades formed at Kathu Pan 1

date.marks: Midpoint of the 511-435 ka estimate for stratified Fauresmith sites (Herries); Porat et al. give a minimum OSL age of 464 ka
date.note: Porat et al. also report a U-series-ESR age with a larger uncertainty and a higher central value (about 540 ka).

events.summary: An in situ Fauresmith assemblage with blades at Kathu Pan 1 has a minimum OSL age of 464 ka and may date to 511-435 ka.
events.body:
> Here we present a minimum OSL age of 464 [@porat-2010, Abstract]

> provides evidence supporting the position that blade production in southern Africa predated the Middle Stone Age [@porat-2010, Abstract]

> this transitional industry maybe as old as 511–435 ka [@herries-2011, Abstract]

events.title: Lebus tuff deposited in the Kapthurin Formation

date.marks: Radiometric date of 465.3 ± 1 ka for the Lebus tuff (Blegen et al. 2018, as cited by Shipton)

events.place: Kapthurin Formation, west of Lake Baringo (Kenya)
events.summary: Volcanic tuff in the Kapthurin Formation, dated to 465.3 ka, lies below the K3 member that holds Acheulean sites with Levallois cores.
events.body: > stratigraphically above the Lebus tuff dated to 465.3 ± 1 ka [@shipton-2022, The Kapthurin Formation Acheulean]

events.title: Hearths at Menez-Dregan I, Brittany

date.marks: ESR date of 465 ± 65 ka for stratigraphic unit 9a

events.summary: Menez-Dregan I yielded hearth traces among the oldest in Europe, ESR-dated for stratigraphic unit 9a to 465 ± 65 ka.
events.body: > The site has yielded globally important traces of hearths that are among the oldest in Europe (465 +/− 65 ka electron spin resonance [ESR] dating for stratigraphic unit [SU] 9a) [@ravon-2022, Introduction]

events.title: Hominin mandible BH-1 deposited at Mala Balanica

date.marks: Midpoint of the 397-525 ka minimum-age range (ESR/U-series and IR/post-IR luminescence)
date.note: These are minimum ages; the mandible could be older.

events.summary: The BH-1 mandible from Mala Balanica has a minimum age of 397-525 ka by ESR/U-series and luminescence dating.
events.body: > provide a minimum age that lies between 397 and 525 ka for the hominin mandible BH-1 from Mala Balanica cave, Serbia [@rink-2013, Abstract]

events.title: Arago 21 cranium (Tautavel Man) dated about 450,000 years old

date.marks: 'About 450,000 years old' as given by the Smithsonian Human Origins Program

events.summary: The Arago 21 cranium from Tautavel, assigned to Homo heidelbergensis, is given an age of about 450,000 years.
events.body:
> About 450,000 years old [@smithsonian-arago21, Exhibit item]

> Tautavel, France [@smithsonian-arago21, Exhibit item]

events.title: Acheulean glacial-stage occupation at Old Park, Canterbury

date.marks: Unit dated 'around 437 ka' (radiometric and palaeomagnetic dating), aligned with MIS 12

events.place: Old Park (Fordwich Pit), Canterbury, Kent (England, UK)
events.summary: A stratigraphic unit at Old Park dated to around 437 ka, aligned with MIS 12, contains fresh flakes (including biface-thinning) showing occupation by Acheulean hominins during a glacial stage.
events.body:
> Two additional artefact-bearing stratigraphic units, dated to around 542 ka and 437 ka, strongly align with the MIS 14 and 12 cold stages, respectively. [@key-2025-2, Abstract]

> The latter unit contains convincing evidence of glacial-stage occupation by Acheulean hominins [@key-2025-2, Abstract]

events.title: Hominins use wooden handheld tools and butcher elephants at Marathousa 1

date.marks: 'ca. 430 ka (MIS12)' per the authors
date.note: Another paper gives the site as ~478,000 to 424,000 years ago.

events.summary: Two wood pieces from Marathousa 1, an alder digging-stick and a small willow/poplar tool, were modified by hominins at a palaeolakeshore in a glacial (MIS 12) refugium.
events.body:
> we present the earliest handheld wooden tools, identified from secure contexts at the site of Marathousa 1, Greece, dated to ca. 430 ka (MIS12) [@milks-2026, Abstract]

> including the manufacture and use of lithic and bone artifacts, alongside butchery of straight-tusked elephants and other fauna [@milks-2026, Significance]

> Marathousa I (~478,000 to 424,000 years ago) [@parfitt-2026, Introduction]

events.title: Sima de los Huesos hominin assemblage accumulates at Atapuerca

date.marks: 'approximately 430,000 years ago' (Arsuaga et al. 2014 dating, as cited by Meyer et al. 2016)
date.note: Earlier estimates placed the Sima de los Huesos fossils around 530 ka; the ~430 ka figure is the more recent one.

events.place: Sima de los Huesos, Sierra de Atapuerca (Spain)
events.summary: An assemblage of 28 hominin individuals was deposited in Sima de los Huesos; the fossils are related to Neanderthals rather than Denisovans.
events.body:
> A unique assemblage of 28 hominin individuals, found in Sima de los Huesos in the Sierra de Atapuerca in Spain, has recently been dated to approximately 430,000 years ago [@meyer-2016, Abstract]

> the Sima de los Huesos hominins were related to Neanderthals rather than to Denisovans [@meyer-2016, Abstract]

> H. heidelbergensis fossils such as those from Sima de los Huesos at 530 ka [@herries-2011, Introduction]

events.title: Occupation of Qesem Cave begins (Acheulo-Yabrudian)

date.marks: Start of the dated sequence 'MIS 11-7 (420-200 ka)'

events.summary: Hominin occupation of Qesem Cave is dated from about 420 ka, with the sequence running to about 200 ka (MIS 11-7).
events.body: > Qesem Cave is a Middle Pleistocene, Acheulo-Yabrudian Cultural Complex site in Israel and well dated to MIS 11-7 (420-200 ka). [@gopher-2017, Summary]

events.title: Anthropogenic fire and hominin cranium at Gruta da Aroeira, Portugal

date.marks: Occupation dated 'ca. 400 ka (Marine Isotope Stage 11)' by the source.

events.place: Gruta da Aroeira, Torres Novas, Portugal
events.summary: Burnt bone, charcoal and possibly quartzite cobbles in layer X at Gruta da Aroeira suggest anthropogenic fires at a site dated to about 400 ka that also yielded a hominin cranium with Acheulean bifaces.
events.body:
> The site of Gruta da Aroeira (Torres Novas, Portugal), with evidence of human occupancy dating to ca. 400 ka (Marine Isotope Stage 11) [@sanz-2020, Abstract]

> suggests the presence of anthropogenic fires at the site, among the oldest such evidence in south-western Europe [@sanz-2020, Abstract]

events.title: Beaver hunting at Bilzingsleben, Germany

date.marks: Site described as 'c. 400,000 years old' (MIS 11) by the authors.

events.summary: Cut marks and a prime-age mortality profile on beaver remains show systematic exploitation of beavers by hominins at Bilzingsleben, a site of about 400,000 years age (MIS 11).
events.body: > cut mark evidence demonstrating systematic exploitation of beavers, identified in the large faunal assemblage from the c. 400,000 years old hominin site Bilzingsleben, in central Germany [@gaudzinski-windheuser-2023, Abstract]

events.title: Burning horizons and heated artefacts at Beeches Pit, Suffolk

date.marks: Project's own round figure 'around 400,000 years ago' (Hoxnian interglacial, MIS 11 context).

events.place: Beeches Pit, West Stow, Suffolk, England (UK)
events.summary: At least three distinct burning horizons, including probable hearths and heated artefacts, were identified at Beeches Pit, in a period of fire-use evidence in East Anglia around 400,000 years ago.
events.body:
> At Beeches Pit, 10 km south-west of Barnham, at least three distinct burning horizons, including probable hearths and heated artefacts, have been identified. [@pab-fire-400ka, Barnham section, Implications]

> In Europe there is occasional evidence of fire-use from around 400,000 years ago [@pab-fire-400ka, Background]

events.title: Evidence of fire-making at Barnham, Suffolk

date.marks: Source describes a '400,000-year-old buried landsurface'; the project page also says 'over 400,000 years ago', with deposits laid down in the Hoxnian interglacial (MIS 11).
date.note: Described by the excavators as over 400,000 years old; the year is a round figure, not a measured age.

events.summary: Heated sediments, fire-cracked flint handaxes and two fragments of iron pyrite on a buried land surface at Barnham are interpreted as evidence of fire-making about 400,000 years ago.
events.body: > Here we present evidence of fire-making on a 400,000-year-old buried landsurface at Barnham (UK), where heated sediments and fire-cracked flint handaxes were found alongside two fragments of iron pyrite [@davis-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Landscape around Olorgesailie becomes more variable about 400,000 years ago

date.marks: Source's own figure 'around 400,000 years ago', from the Koora drill core record; −400,000.

events.summary: A Koora-basin drill core shows the environment of the southern Kenya Rift became more variable around 400,000 years ago, when tectonic activity fragmented the landscape.
events.body: > the environment in this part of Africa became more variable around 400,000 years ago, when tectonic activity fragmented the landscape. [@smithsonian-olorgesailie-2020, News release, 21 Oct 2020]

events.title: Levallois cores in Acheulean context at Kapthurin Formation, Kenya

date.marks: Tephrochronology, '~ 400 ka', as summarised by White et al. 2024 citing Tryon et al. 2006, Blegen et al. 2018 and Shipton 2022.

events.summary: The earliest known cores conforming fully to the Levallois concept are reported from an Acheulean context in the Kapthurin Formation, dated by tephrochronology to about 400 ka.
events.body: > The earliest known cores that fully conform to Boëda’s Levallois concept are found in an Acheulean context in the Kapthurin Formation, Kenya, dated by tephrochronology to ~ 400 ka [@white-2024, Introduction, 'When Is Levallois Not Levallois?']

events.title: Terra Amata site, Nice, dated about 400,000 years ago

date.marks: Age given as 'About 400,000 years old' in the Smithsonian exhibit entry; method not stated there.
date.note: The shelter interpretation of the post holes is the excavator's reading.

events.summary: The Terra Amata site, with post holes and other evidence interpreted as multiple shelters, is given an age of about 400,000 years.
events.body:
> Scientists found post holes and other evidence of multiple shelters at this site. [@smithsonian-terra-amata, Exhibit item]

> About 400,000 years old [@smithsonian-terra-amata, Exhibit item]

events.title: Acheulian ends and Middle Palaeolithic emerges at Attirampakkam, India

date.marks: Luminescence dating, 385 ± 64 ka; converted to BCE as −385,000 with the stated error as range.
date.note: The Middle Palaeolithic at the site is reported to continue until 172 ± 41 ka.

events.summary: Luminescence dating at Attirampakkam dates the shift from Acheulian to Middle Palaeolithic technology to about 385 ± 64 ka, much earlier than conventionally presumed for South Asia.
events.body: > Luminescence dating at the stratified prehistoric site of Attirampakkam, India, has shown that processes signifying the end of the Acheulian culture and the emergence of a Middle Palaeolithic culture occurred at 385 ± 64 thousand years ago (ka) [@akhilesh-2018, Abstract]

events.title: Homo naledi remains deposited in the Dinaledi Chamber, Rising Star Cave

date.marks: Placed at the older bound of the reported 236–335 ka depositional window (US-ESR on teeth combined with U-Th on the oldest overlying flowstone).
date.note: The wider sediment unit is interpreted as deposited between 236 and 414 ka; a minimum-age scenario for the teeth gives about 200 ka. The authors favour the maximum-age scenario.

events.place: Rising Star Cave (Dinaledi Chamber), South Africa
events.summary: Combined OSL, U-Th, palaeomagnetic and US-ESR dating constrains the deposition of Homo naledi fossils to between 236 and 335 ka.
events.body:
> we have constrained the depositional age of Homo naledi to a period between 236 ka and 335 ka [@dirks-2017, Abstract]

> New ages for flowstone, sediments and fossil bones from the Dinaledi Chamber are presented. [@dirks-2017, Abstract]

events.title: Levallois and biface technology used together at Nor Geghi 1, Armenia

date.marks: Layers correlated to OIS 9e (335 to 325 ka) using 40Ar/39Ar ages of bracketing basalts and tephra, plus stratigraphy.
date.note: The sediments are bracketed by basalts of about 441 and 197 ka; the 335–325 ka age is a correlation to OIS 9e.

events.summary: Nor Geghi 1 has obsidian assemblages with both bifaces and Levallois cores in alluvial layers correlated with OIS 9e (335–325 ka), described as the earliest synchronic use of both technologies outside Africa.
events.body:
> Our data from Nor Geghi 1, Armenia, record the earliest synchronic use of bifacial and Levallois technology outside Africa [@adler-2014, Abstract]

> deposition of and pedogenesis within Units 3 to 2 with OIS 9e (335 to 325 ka) [@adler-2014, p. 1611]

> Seventeen of these cores conform to criteria that define Levallois technology [@adler-2014, p. 1611]

events.title: People at Olorgesailie enter the Middle Stone Age about 320,000 years ago

date.marks: Source's own figure 'around 320,000 years ago' (Smithsonian summary of Potts and colleagues' work); −320,000.

events.place: Olorgesailie, southern Kenya Rift Valley, Kenya
events.summary: After about 700,000 years of handaxe use, people at Olorgesailie began making smaller tools and projectiles, trading with distant groups and using colouring materials from around 320,000 years ago.
events.body: > Then, beginning around 320,000 years ago, people living there entered the Middle Stone Age, crafting smaller, more sophisticated weapons, including projectiles. [@smithsonian-olorgesailie-2020, News release, 21 Oct 2020]

events.title: Purfleet MIS 9 site with simple prepared cores, Essex

date.marks: Site described as '~ 320-ka (MIS 9)' by White et al. 2024.
date.note: Earlier interpretations (White and Ashton 2003) saw early Levallois here; White et al. 2024 reject this.

events.summary: The roughly 320 ka (MIS 9) Purfleet site yielded simple prepared cores once read as proto-Levallois; a 2024 re-examination finds no true Levallois concept in MIS 9 Britain.
events.body:
> The ~ 320-ka (MIS 9) site at Purfleet (Essex), England, has played a pivotal role in these discussions [@white-2024, Introduction]

> we find no evidence for a true Levallois concept in MIS 11 or MIS 9 in Britain. [@white-2024, Abstract]

events.title: Homo sapiens fossils and Middle Stone Age artefacts at Jebel Irhoud dated to about 315 ka

date.marks: Weighted mean of thermoluminescence ages of heated flint, 315 ± 34 ka (thousand years before present); converted to BCE as −315,000, with the ± 34 ka error as range.
date.note: A separate US-ESR date on an Irhoud 3 mandible tooth gives 286 ± 32 ka, overlapping the TL result.

events.summary: Thermoluminescence dating of fire-heated flints places Middle Stone Age artefacts and associated H. sapiens fossils at Jebel Irhoud at about 315,000 years ago, with a supporting US-ESR date on a mandible tooth.
events.body:
> A weighted average age places these Middle Stone Age artefacts and fossils at 315 ± 34 thousand years ago. [@richter-2017, Abstract]

> determined by thermoluminescence dating, of fire-heated flint artefacts obtained from new excavations at the Middle Stone Age site of Jebel Irhoud, Morocco [@richter-2017, Abstract]

events.title: Fireplaces in upper deposits of Qesem Cave, Israel

date.marks: Placed at the midpoint of the 420–200 ka range given for the site; the individual fireplaces are not dated more closely in this source.
date.note: The range is wide; the fireplaces come from the upper deposits, so they may fall in the later part of it.

events.summary: In-situ fireplaces with wood ash, burnt bones and lithics in the upper deposits of Qesem Cave are cited as undisputed fire evidence dated to 420–200 ka.
events.body: > the earliest undisputed evidence dates to 420–200 ka, as exemplified by the in-situ fireplaces (wood ash) associated with burnt bones and lithics found in the upper deposits of Qesem Cave (Israel) [@sanz-2020, Introduction]

events.title: Hominin occupation of Denisova Cave possibly begins

date.marks: 'As early as 300,000 years ago' as stated by the source, based on optical dating of cave sediments.
date.note: The source hedges: the stone tools only suggest occupation may have begun this early. Denisovan presence is attested from at least 200,000 years ago.

events.summary: Stone tools in the deepest deposits of Denisova Cave suggest human occupation may have begun as early as 300,000 years ago, according to the 2019 optical and radiocarbon dating studies.
events.body: > with stone tools in the deepest deposits suggesting human occupation may have begun as early as 300,000 years ago. [@oxford-denisova, main text]

events.title: Hualongdong hominin fossils buried in cave deposits, Anhui, China

date.marks: Burial age of about 300,000 years (280,000–330,000 years) from biostratigraphy and U-Th dating of speleothems and animal teeth, spanning MIS 9e to 8c.
date.note: U-series dates show the carbonate debris is no older than 331 ka and that cave collapse and reaccumulation occurred no later than 285 ka.

events.summary: Human fossils including a nearly complete skull were buried at Hualongdong about 300,000 years ago, with associated lithics and mammal remains; excavated in 2014–2015.
events.body:
> Between 2014 and 2015, abundant human fossils dated to about 300 ka were found in the Hualongdong (HLD) site, Anhui province, South China. [@wu-2025, Abstract]

> the burial age of the fossils at HLD is approximately 300,000 years (280,000–330,000 years), spanning Marine Isotope Stages 9e to 8c [@wu-2025, Introduction]

events.title: Red ochre deposited with Middle Stone Age assemblage at Kapthurin GnJh-15

date.marks: Assemblage date given as 285,000 b.p. by Barham (2002), citing McBrearty (2001); a symbol before the figure is garbled in the digitised text.
date.note: The printed qualifier before 285,000 is unreadable in the text read; it may mark a minimum age.

events.summary: More than 70 pieces of red ochre, weighing over 5 kg, occur at GnJh-15 with an early Middle Stone Age assemblage dated to about 285,000 years ago, as reported by McBrearty and cited by Barham.
events.body: > more than 70 pieces of “red ochre” with a total weight of more than 5 kg occur with an archaeological assemblage dated to 1 285,000 [@barham-2002, p. 189]

events.title: Hominin occupation at Gademotta, Ethiopia, with obsidian points used as projectile tips

date.marks: Minimum age of >279±2 ka from 40Ar/39Ar dating of the lowermost occupation horizon (sites ETH-72-8B and GDM7); a minimum age, not a point estimate.
date.note: The 279 ka figure is a minimum age for the lowest horizon, so the occupation could be older. Dates were recalculated with updated decay constants.

events.summary: The lowest occupation horizon at the Gademotta type-site is dated to more than 279,000 years ago; pointed obsidian artefacts from the Gademotta Formation are interpreted as hafted javelin tips.
events.body:
> pointed stone artifacts from Ethiopia were used as projectile weapons (in the form of hafted javelin tips) as early as >279,000 years ago. [@sahle-2013, Abstract]

> The lowermost occupation horizon, sampled by sites ETH-72-8B and GDM7 in the type-site, has recently been redated by [@sahle-2013, Materials and Methods]

events.title: Florisbad hominin cranium dated to about 259 ka

date.marks: About 259 ka as cited by Herries (2011) from Grün et al. (1996) dating of the cranium; Berger et al. (2017) tabulate 224–294 ka.
date.note: Dates come from direct dating of the Florisbad cranium (Grün et al. 1996); the quoted range is about 259 ± 35 ka.

events.summary: The Florisbad partial cranium, type specimen of Homo helmei, comes from a deposit with Middle Stone Age technology and is dated to about 259 ka, with a published range of 224–294 ka.
events.body:
> the Florisbad hominin skull (the type specimen of Homo helmei [11]) is associated with a “Florisian Land Mammal Age” [@herries-2011-2, Section 1 (Introduction)]

> faunal assemblage and MSA technology and is dated to ~259 ka [@herries-2011-2, Section 1 (Introduction)]

> Florisbad Partial cranium South Africa 224–294 Grün et al. (1996) [@berger-2017, Table of Middle Pleistocene hominin sites]

events.title: Jinniushan hominin skeleton deposited in cave fissure, northeastern China

date.marks: About 260,000 years ago, from ESR and uranium-series dating of animal teeth from Layer 7 (Rosenberg et al. 2006); placement year approximate (about 260 ka).
date.note: Earlier published dates for the specimen were younger but averaged levels higher in the section than the human remains, according to Rosenberg et al.

events.summary: A partial skeleton including a cranium, pelvis and ulna was deposited in Layer 7 of the Jinniushan cave fissure, dated by ESR and U-series on animal teeth to about 260,000 years ago.
events.body:
> Electron-spin resonance and uranium series dating of animal teeth from Layer 7 suggest a date of ≈260,000 years ago [@rosenberg-2006, Background and Dates]

> The Jinniushan specimen was discovered near the town of Yinkou in Liaoning Province in northeastern China [@rosenberg-2006, Background and Dates]

events.title: Hominin remains deposited at Biache-Saint-Vaast, northern France

date.marks: ESR estimate of 253 ka (Yokoyama 1989, cited by Martín-Francés et al. 2022); other estimates: OSL 175 ± 13 ka, ESR/U-series mean ca. 240 ka, one tooth 332 ± 28 ka.
date.note: Dating is disputed: pollen and fauna indicate MIS 7 (240–190 ka); the recent ESR/U-series mean is ca. 240 ka (just outside this period), while the 253 ka ESR age and a 332 ka tooth age fall earlier.

events.summary: Two Middle Pleistocene hominin individuals were found with rich lithic and faunal remains at Biache-Saint-Vaast; dating estimates run from about 175 to 332 ka, with a recent mean of ca. 240 ka.
events.body:
> First dating analyses, including OSL and ESR, provided ages of 175±13 ka (Huxtable and Aikten 1988 ) and 253 + 53/– 37 ka (Yokoyama 1989 ), respectively. [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

> provided a mean age of ca. 240 ka (Bahain et al. 2015 ), correlating the human occupation to MIS 7c [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

> The hominin remains were associated to a rich lithic and faunal context. [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

> the dating result of 332 ± 28 ka obtained for the only tooth of the study that do not show uranium leaching [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

events.title: Denisovan mtDNA first appears in Denisova Cave sediments from about 250 ka

date.marks: 'From ~250 ka' per Jacobs et al. (2025), based on optical dating of cave sediments across three chambers and mtDNA from sediment samples; placed at the end of the requested period.
date.note: The authors note some layer ages (e.g. layer 17 in South Chamber) are poorly constrained; the year is a lower bound for the onset of the Denisovan sediment DNA record, not a date for any one event.

events.place: Denisova Cave, Altai, southern Siberia, Russia
events.summary: Sediment DNA and optical dating indicate that the oldest layers containing Denisovan mitochondrial DNA at Denisova Cave accumulated from about 250 ka, with early Middle Palaeolithic stone tools.
aliases: Earliest Denisovan DNA in Denisova Cave sediments
events.body:
> The oldest layers with Denisovan mtDNA accumulated from ~250 ka [@jacobs-2025, Discussion]

> Denisova Cave in southern Siberia is the only site known to have been occupied by Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans. [@jacobs-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Heat-altered fragments at Maastricht-Belvédère, dated to about 250 ka

date.marks: About 250 ka, as stated in a review of Middle Pleistocene fire evidence.
date.note: Interpretation as a combustion structure is disputed.

events.summary: The Middle Palaeolithic site of Maastricht-Belvédère, dated to about 250 ka, yielded concentrations of heat-altered fragments in two groups; one researcher proposes a natural origin for them.
events.body:
> Maastricht-Belvédère (The Netherlands), dated to 250 ka and associated with Middle Paleolithic industry [@stancampiano-2023, Past records of fire within human evolution]

> although Roebroeks 25 proposes a natural origin for such concentrations [@stancampiano-2023, Past records of fire within human evolution]

events.title: Hearth-like combustion structures at Acheulean site of Valdocarros II, Madrid

date.marks: Site dated to MIS 8/7 (~245 kya); occupation range 235–285 kya, with amino-acid racemization ages of 254 ± 47 and 262 ± 07 ka.
date.note: The site is placed between about 285 and 235 ka; 245 ka is the figure used in the title of the study.

events.summary: Lipid biomarkers of incomplete combustion in two hearth-like structures at Valdocarros II are interpreted as evidence of human-controlled fire in an Acheulean context dated to about 245 ka.
events.body:
> Valdocarros II site, one of the largest European Acheulean sites in Spain dated to marine isotopic stage (MIS) 8/7 (~ 245 kya) [@stancampiano-2023, Abstract]

> The presence of combustion byproducts suggests the presence of anthropogenic (controlled) fires at Valdocarros—one of the oldest evidence of fire use in Europe-in association with Acheulean tools and bones. [@stancampiano-2023, Abstract]

> with evidence of human occupancy dating to a range between 235 and 285 kya (MIS 7/8) [@stancampiano-2023, Valdocarros II site]

events.title: Saccopastore Neanderthal skulls assigned to early MIS 7 gravels, Rome

date.marks: Age assigned by correlating Aniene-valley aggradational sediments with sea-level rise at the onset of MIS 7, using published 40Ar/39Ar ages; lowest gravel layer about 245 ka.
date.note: These skulls were formerly attributed to 130,000–80,000 years ago; the sedimentary succession in the area spans 295–220 ka.

events.summary: Chronostratigraphic correlation with sea-level rise assigns the gravel layer holding one Saccopastore Neanderthal skull to about 245 ka, and the uppermost gravel layer to about 220 ka.
events.body:
> we assign ages of 245 ka and 220 ka to the Neanderthal skulls recovered within the lowest and the uppermost gravel layer at Saccopastore, respectively. [@marra-2017, Introduction]

> An age ranging from130,000–80,000 years BP was attributed to these skulls [@marra-2017, Introduction]

events.title: Late Middle Pleistocene deposits at Wadi Lazalim dated by IRSL, southern Tunisia

date.marks: pIRIR290 single-grain feldspar ages: layer 4a 252 ± 23 ka, 4b 232 ± 22 ka, 5 234 ± 22 ka.
date.note: The authors note low resolution; the whole sequence spans about 300–130 ka and layers could belong to MIS 7–8.

events.summary: IRSL ages for layers 4a, 4b and 5 at site 15/1 of the Wadi Lazalim sequence, which has yielded Middle Stone Age human occupation evidence, fall at about 232–252 ka.
events.body:
> the four ages obtained from layers 4a (252 ± 23 ka), 4b (232 ± 22 ka), 5 (234 ± 22 ka) and 9/10 (207 ± 21 ka), are potentially slightly older and could be included in MIS 7–8. [@cancellieri-2022, Results]

> which has yielded evidence for human occupations bracketed between ca. 300–130 ka [@cancellieri-2022, Abstract]

events.title: Shala volcano eruption dated 233 ± 22 ka, giving a minimum age for Omo I fossils

date.marks: Age of the proximal deposits of the Shala eruption, 233 ± 22 kyr (40Ar/39Ar dating), a minimum age for the Omo fossils.
date.note: Omo I was previously dated to about 197 kyr from the Nakaa'kire Tuff; the new result is a minimum age and the fossils are older than the eruption.

events.place: Shala volcano, Main Ethiopian Rift; Omo-Kibish Formation, Ethiopia
events.summary: Geochemical correlation links the Kamoya's Hominid Site Tuff, which overlies the Omo I fossil-bearing member of the Omo-Kibish Formation, to a major explosive eruption of Shala volcano, dated 233 ± 22 kyr.
events.body:
> link the Kamoya’s Hominid Site (KHS) Tuff 9 , which conclusively overlies the member of the Omo-Kibish Formation that contains Omo I, with a major explosive eruption of Shala volcano [@vidal-2022, Abstract]

> By dating the proximal deposits of this eruption, we obtain a new minimum age for the Omo fossils of 233 ± 22 kyr. [@vidal-2022, Abstract]

events.title: Burned bone accumulates in layers C and D at La Cotte de Saint-Brelade, Jersey

date.marks: Chronology of ca. 230 ka as stated in a review.

events.summary: High densities of burned bone are present in layers C and D at La Cotte de Saint-Brelade, with a chronology of about 230 ka, though without evidence of hearths.
events.body: > at La Cotte de Saint Brelade (Jersey), with a chronology, ca. 230 ka, high densities of burned bone were present in layers C and D though no evidence of hearths [@stancampiano-2023, Past records of fire within human evolution]

events.title: Hearths at Bolomor Cave, Valencia, dated MIS 7c

date.marks: 228 ± 53 ka by amino-acid racemization (AAR), MIS 7c, as reported in a review.

events.summary: Bolomor Cave records repeated use of fire, with hearths in levels II, IV, XI and XIII; one level's hearths are dated to MIS 7c (228 ± 53 ka by amino-acid racemization).
events.body: > documented reiterative use of fire due to the presence of hearths at levels II, IV, XI, and XIII, in this level the hearths dated to MIS 7c (228 ± 53 ka by AAR) [@stancampiano-2023, Past records of fire within human evolution]

events.title: Early Neanderthal fossils and tools deposited in Pontnewydd Cave, Wales

date.marks: About 225,000 BP (MIS 7), as stated in the Encyclopedia of Global Archaeology entry; placed at the edge of the requested period.
date.note: Other summaries give a range of dates for the deposits; 225,000 years is the commonly cited figure.

events.summary: Early Neanderthal fossils, stone tools and fauna were washed into Pontnewydd Cave by debris or mudflows around 225,000 years ago, in MIS 7.
events.body:
> Dating back to around 225,000 BP during marine isotope stage 7 (MIS 7), the deposits are not in situ but washed into the cave during debris or mudflows. [@walker-2020, Definition]

> Evolutionary early Neanderthal fossils, associated stone tools, and a contemporary faunal assemblage have all been excavated from deposits within Pontnewydd Cave. [@walker-2020, Definition]

events.title: Middle Stone Age lithics appear at Amanzi Springs, South Africa, by 230 ± 18 ka

date.marks: Onset of the MSA by 230 ± 18 ka (1σ; multiple luminescence methods); year placed within the 1σ range because the central value lies just outside this period.

events.place: Amanzi Springs Area 7, Eastern Cape (South Africa)
events.summary: Luminescence dating of a stratified Acheulian-to-MSA sequence at the open-air site of Amanzi Springs places the emergence of the MSA there around 230 ± 18 ka, earlier than previously documented on the southern coast.
events.body:
> We show that the MSA emerged around 230 ± 18 ka, significantly earlier than previously documented along the southern coast. [@blackwood-2026, Abstract]

> a stratified sequence of Acheulian to MSA lithic assemblages from the open-air site of Amanzi Springs covering the period between ~ 379 to 95 ka [@blackwood-2026, Abstract]

events.title: Neanderthal introgression into Denisovans in the Altai, as early as 250-200 ka

date.marks: Range 250-200 ka given by the source for the introgression; placed at its midpoint.
date.note: Dates for Denisova 2 itself are debated (122-194 ka by one Bayesian model; as early as 280 ka by optical ages).

events.place: Altai region (Siberia, Russia), possibly near Denisova Cave
events.summary: Genomic analysis of Denisova 2 shows Neanderthal ancestry from an introgression about 1500 years before she lived, as early as 250-200 ka; the location of the interbreeding is unknown.
events.body:
> she had Neanderthal ancestry deriving from an introgression ~1500 years before she lived, as early as 250-200 ka. [@brown-2022, Discussion]

> Although it is not possible to tell where these interbreeding events occurred [@brown-2022, Discussion]

events.title: Neanderthal MIS 7 occupation of Abri du Maras, Ardèche

date.marks: MIS 7 occupation between 247 ± 34 and 223 ± 33 ka (Bayesian model); year placed near the later end of the span, which falls within this period.

events.summary: Bayesian modelling of OSL, ESR/U-series and radiocarbon ages shows Neanderthals used the Maras rock shelter as a long-term residence during MIS 7, between 247 ± 34 and 223 ± 33 ka.
events.body:
> the site has been used as a long-term residence by Neanderthals, specifically during three interglacial periods: first during marine isotopic stage (MIS) 7, between 247 ± 34 and 223 ± 33 ka [@richard-2024, Abstract]

> Located in the Ardèche gorge (Fig. 1), the Abri du Maras [@richard-2024, Site description]

events.title: Omo I (Omo-Kibish) Homo sapiens fossils given a minimum age of 233 \u00b1 22 kyr

date.marks: Published minimum age of 233 ± 22 kyr for the fossils (40Ar/39Ar age of the Shala Qi2 eruption linked to the overlying KHS Tuff). The central value lies just outside this period, so the year is placed inside the ±22 kyr range.
