date.note: The fossils were previously dated to about 197 kyr; the new age is a minimum age and its central value (233 ka) is slightly older than this period's start.

events.summary: Tephra geochemistry and 40Ar/39Ar dating of the Shala Qi2 eruption give a new minimum age of 233 \u00b1 22 kyr for the Omo fossils, older than the ~197 kyr usually cited.
events.body:
> By dating the proximal deposits of this eruption, we obtain a new minimum age for the Omo fossils of 233 ± 22 kyr. [@vidal-2022-2, Abstract]

> The ages that are generally reported for these fossils are around 197 thousand years (kyr) for the Kibish Omo I [@vidal-2022-2, Abstract]

events.title: Qi2 ignimbrite eruption of Shala volcano, Main Ethiopian Rift

date.marks: Preferred composite 40Ar/39Ar eruption age of 233 ± 22 kyr (2σ); placed within the range because the central value lies just outside this period.

events.summary: A major explosive eruption of Shala volcano, dated by 40Ar/39Ar to 233 ± 22 kyr, is geochemically linked to the KHS Tuff that overlies the Omo I fossil-bearing member in Kibish.
events.body:
> with a major explosive eruption of Shala volcano in the Main Ethiopian Rift. [@vidal-2022-2, Abstract]

> yielding a preferred composite eruption age of 233 ± 22 kyr [@vidal-2022-2, Fig. 2 caption]

events.title: Specialised hornfels procurement begins at Jojosi, South Africa, about 220 ka

date.marks: Start of the Jojosi lithic assemblages at ~220 ka (luminescence-based chronology in the source).

events.summary: Stratified open-air assemblages with abundant refits show early modern humans repeatedly visiting a hornfels source to reduce and export tool stone from about 220 ka to about 110 ka.
events.body:
> lithic assemblages with abundant refits dating from ~220 ka to ~110 ka for the reduction and export of a single tool stone. [@will-2026, Abstract]

> Archaeological excavations coupled with multidisciplinary analyses at Jojosi in South Africa demonstrate that early modern humans undertook specific, repeated visits to a raw material source [@will-2026, Abstract]

events.title: Hominin remains deposited at Biache-Saint-Vaast during MIS 7, about 240 ka

date.marks: MIS 7 interval (240-190 ka) given for the deposit; year is its midpoint. ESR/U-series on fauna gives ca. 240 ka (MIS 7c).
date.note: Other results: OSL 175 ± 13 ka, ESR 253 +53/-37 ka, and 332 ± 28 ka for one tooth; an older chronology is not excluded.

events.summary: Hominin remains with Neanderthal affinities from Biache-Saint-Vaast, associated with rich lithic and faunal remains, are dated to MIS 7 (between 240 and 190 ka); ESR/U-series gives a mean of about 240 ka.
events.body:
> indicate a deposit episode for the human remains during the MIS 7 (between 240 and 190 ka [@martin-frances-2022, Introduction]

> eleven hominin dental remains recovered from the MP, ca. 240 ka, French site of Biache-Saint-Vaast (BSV) [@martin-frances-2022, Abstract]

events.title: Apidima 1 cranium from Apidima Cave dated to more than 210 ka

date.marks: Minimum age of more than 210 thousand years ago by U-series radiometric dating, as stated by the authors.
date.note: This is a minimum age; the true age could be older.

events.summary: U-series dating gives Apidima 1, a cranium with a mixture of modern human and primitive features, an age of more than 210,000 years; Apidima 2 from the same cave is more than 170,000 years old and Neanderthal-like.
events.body:
> Apidima 1 dates to more than 210 thousand years ago and presents a mixture of modern human and primitive features. [@harvati-2019, Abstract]

> Two fossilized human crania (Apidima 1 and Apidima 2) from Apidima Cave, southern Greece [@harvati-2019, Abstract]

events.title: Denisovan remains deposited in layer 15 of Denisova Cave East Chamber at about 200 ka

date.marks: About 200 ka (205-192 ka at 68.2% or 217-187 ka at 95% probability), Bayesian modelling of optical ages for layer 15. Placed at the end of this period.
date.note: Earlier work estimated Denisova 2 at 122-194 ka, or as early as 280 ka from optical ages only.

events.summary: Three bones from the lowest archaeological layer of the East Chamber carry Denisovan mtDNA; layer 15 is dated to about 200 ka, making them the oldest securely dated Denisovan evidence.
events.body:
> and are the oldest securely dated evidence of Denisovans, at 200 ka (205-192 ka at 68.2% or 217-187 ka at 95% probability). [@brown-2022, Abstract]

> The specimens with the Denisovan mtDNAs (19, 20 and 21) all come from layer 15 of the East Chamber. [@brown-2022, Discussion]

events.title: Genome of a Denisovan man who lived about 200,000 years ago, from Denisova Cave

date.marks: About 200,000 years ago, as given in the preprint's title and abstract; placed at the end of this period.
date.note: Preprint; the age is the authors' approximate figure.

events.summary: A second high-coverage Denisovan genome, reconstructed from a molar found at Denisova Cave, is reported from an individual who lived around 200,000 years ago.
events.body:
> A high-coverage genome from a 200,000-year-old Denisovan [@peyregne-2025, Title]

> reconstructed from a molar found at Denisova Cave. [@peyregne-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Schöningen Spear Horizon with wooden hunting spears dated to about 200 ka

date.marks: Late MIS 7, ~200 ka, from amino acid geochronology of fossils from the find-bearing deposits and a regional chronostratigraphic reassessment; placed at the end of this period.
date.note: Earlier estimates were about 400,000 and later about 300,000 years; the 200 ka age is a 2025 revision.

events.summary: Amino acid geochronology and regional chronostratigraphy place the Schöningen 13II-4 Spear Horizon, with wooden spears and butchered horses, in late MIS 7 at about 200,000 years, rather than 400 or 300 ka.
events.body:
> Together with a reassessment of regional Middle Pleistocene chronostratigraphy, these data place the Schöningen spears at ~200,000 years. [@hutson-2025, Abstract]

> we suggest a late MIS 7 age around ~200 ka for the Spear Horizon [@hutson-2025, Discussion]

> holds title to the most complete Paleolithic wooden hunting spears ever discovered [@hutson-2025, Abstract]

events.title: Occupation of Qesem Cave ends, possibly around 200 ka

date.marks: 230Th/234U dates on speleothems; the excavators say the end of occupation is 'possibly around 200 ka'; the earliest/latest bounds are illustrative.
date.note: The excavators describe the overall Acheulo-Yabrudian chronology (400–200 ka) as still needing refinement.

events.summary: Uranium-thorium dates on speleothems suggest occupation of Qesem Cave, an Acheulo-Yabrudian site of the terminal Lower Palaeolithic, ended possibly around 200,000 years ago.
events.body: > 230Th/234U dates on speleothems suggest that the occupation of the cave began before 382 ka and ended possibly around 200 ka. [@qesem-project-intro, Introduction]

events.title: Oldest grass bedding layer laid at Border Cave

date.marks: About 200 ka, from luminescence ages on the site's sedimentary sequence as reported by the excavators (2018–2019 work).

events.summary: Grass mats or bedding layers are preserved throughout Border Cave's sequence; the oldest dates to about 200,000 years ago.
events.body: > Grass mats/bedding layers are preserved throughout the sequence, the oldest of which dates to ∼200 ka. [@backwell-2022, Abstract]

events.title: Neanderthals first appear in Denisova Cave

date.marks: 'Shortly after 200 ka' per optical dating of sediments and sediment mtDNA across the cave's three chambers; the year is a placement just after 200 ka, not a source figure.
date.note: The source gives only 'shortly after 200 ka'; the exact placement year here is a convention.

events.summary: Optical dating of sediments and ancient DNA indicate that Neanderthals first appeared at Denisova Cave shortly after about 200,000 years ago, after Denisovans were already present.
events.body: > Neanderthals first appeared shortly after 200 ka [@jacobs-2025-2, Discussion]

events.title: Homo sapiens maxilla deposited at Misliya Cave, Mount Carmel

date.marks: Mean age of dated teeth and flint tools, about 177,000–194,000 years old as reported by the excavators (Tel Aviv University team, 2018); other summaries give 175,000–200,000 years.
date.note: Reports give ranges between about 175,000 and 200,000 years ago depending on the summary; the 177–194 ka range is the excavators' average age for the specimens.

events.summary: A fossil upper jaw with Homo sapiens features, found with flint tools in Misliya Cave, was dated to roughly 177,000–194,000 years ago, older than earlier modern human fossils known outside Africa.
events.body:
> The researchers dated teeth from the jaw and flint tools found with the remains, obtaining an average age for the specimens of about 177,000-194,000 years old. [@mcnish-2018, Science news, 25 Jan 2018]

> The team found part of a fossil human jaw with anatomical features that correspond to the modern human species Homo sapiens, as opposed to other pre-modern humans such as Neanderthals. [@mcnish-2018, Science news, 25 Jan 2018]

events.title: Neanderthal-period stalagmite structures built deep in Bruniquel Cave

date.marks: Uranium-series age of 176.5 thousand years (±2.1 thousand) on stalagmite regrowths, burnt bone and stalagmite tips; placed at the edge of the period within the error range
date.note: The central estimate (176.5 ka) lies just before the start of the requested window; the ±2.1 ka error range straddles it, so the placement year is the window boundary.

events.summary: Annular constructions of broken stalagmites with traces of fire, 336 m from the cave entrance, were dated by uranium series to about 176.5 thousand years (±2.1).
events.body:
> Uranium-series dating of stalagmite regrowths on the structures and on burnt bone, combined with the dating of stalagmite tips in the structures, give a reliable and replicated age of 176.5 thousand years (±2.1 thousand years) [@jaubert-2016, Abstract]

> Their presence at 336 metres from the entrance of the cave indicates that humans from this period had already mastered the underground environment [@jaubert-2016, Abstract]

events.title: Apidima 2 cranium dated to more than 170,000 years ago

date.marks: Minimum age (>170 ka) from U-series radiometric dating
date.note: A minimum age; the younger limit is not given in the cited abstract.

events.summary: U-series dating showed the Neanderthal-like Apidima 2 cranium from southern Greece to be more than 170 thousand years old.
events.body:
> Apidima 2 dates to more than 170 thousand years ago and has a Neanderthal-like morphological pattern. [@harvati-2019, Abstract]

> Two fossilized human crania (Apidima 1 and Apidima 2) from Apidima Cave, southern Greece [@harvati-2019, Abstract]

events.title: Pigment use and bladelet production at Pinnacle Point 13B

date.marks: About 164 kyr ago (±12 kyr), same dating as the shellfish evidence

events.place: Pinnacle Point Cave 13B, Mossel Bay, South Africa
events.summary: Pigment use and modification, and bladelet stone tool production, are reported at Pinnacle Point alongside early marine resource use at about 164 thousand years ago.
events.body:
> Coincident with this diet and habitat expansion is an early use and modification of pigment, probably for symbolic behaviour, as well as the production of bladelet stone tool technology [@marean-2007, Abstract]

> by ∼164 kyr ago (±12 kyr) at Pinnacle Point [@marean-2007, Abstract]

events.title: Shellfish use at Pinnacle Point Cave 13B, South Africa

date.marks: About 164 kyr ago (±12 kyr), dating by Marean et al. (U-series and OSL)

events.place: Pinnacle Point Cave 13B, Mossel Bay, South Africa
events.summary: By about 164 thousand years ago (±12) at Pinnacle Point on the south coast of South Africa, humans had expanded their diet to include marine resources.
events.body: > Here we show that by ∼164 kyr ago (±12 kyr) at Pinnacle Point (on the south coast of South Africa) humans expanded their diet to include marine resources [@marean-2007, Abstract]

events.title: Silcrete heat treatment at Pinnacle Point

date.marks: 'As early as 164 ka' per Brown et al. 2009 (luminescence and other dating of the Pinnacle Point deposits)
date.note: Brown et al. give 164 ka as the earliest appearance; the marine-resource layers at the site carry an uncertainty of ±12 kyr in Marean et al. 2007.

events.place: Pinnacle Point, Mossel Bay, South Africa
events.summary: Analysis of silcrete tools indicates heat treatment to improve flaking appeared as early as 164 ka at Pinnacle Point, becoming predominant by about 72 ka.
events.body: > Heat treatment predominates among silcrete tools at ~72 thousand years ago (ka) and appears as early as 164 ka at Pinnacle Point, on the south coast of South Africa. [@brown-2009, p. 859, abstract]

events.title: Xiahe Denisovan mandible dated to at least 160,000 years ago

date.marks: Minimum age of 160 thousand years from U-series dating of the adhering carbonate matrix
date.note: This is a minimum age; the mandible could be older.

events.place: Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe, Gansu, China
events.summary: A hominin mandible from Baishiya Karst Cave on the Tibetan Plateau, identified as Denisovan by ancient protein analysis, was dated by U-series on adhering carbonate to at least 160 thousand years old.
events.body:
> We determine the mandible to be at least 160 thousand years old through U-series dating of an adhering carbonate matrix. [@chen-2019, Abstract]

> Here we report a Denisovan mandible, identified by ancient protein analysis 9 , 10 , found on the Tibetan Plateau in Baishiya Karst Cave, Xiahe, Gansu, China. [@chen-2019, Abstract]

events.title: Herto hominid crania deposited at Middle Awash, Ethiopia

date.marks: Radioisotopic dating (40Ar/39Ar) to between 160,000 and 154,000 years ago; midpoint used

events.summary: Fossil hominid crania from Herto, radioisotopically dated to between 160,000 and 154,000 years ago, were described as probable immediate ancestors of anatomically modern humans.
events.body:
> Radioisotopically dated to between 160,000 and 154,000 years ago [@white-2003, Abstract]

> They therefore represent the probable immediate ancestors of anatomically modern humans. [@white-2003, Abstract]

events.title: Altamura Neanderthal skeleton, dated by U/Th between about 172 and 130 ka

date.marks: U/Th dating of the calcite covering the skeleton; the range 172 ± 15 to 130.1 ± 1.9 ka is a span of ages, with a midpoint used as the placement year
date.note: The source gives a wide range rather than a single age; the placement year is a midpoint.

events.summary: The Altamura Neanderthal skeleton, embedded in cave concretions, has been dated by U/Th to between 172 ± 15 and 130.1 ± 1.9 ka.
events.body: > The Neanderthal skeleton has been dated by U/Th between 172 ± 15 and 130.1 ± 1.9 ka (4). [@buzi-2025, Introduction]

events.title: Stones set up in the centre of Stonehenge

date.marks: English Heritage's approximate date ("about 2500 BC") for the setting up of the stones in the centre of the monument.

events.summary: According to English Heritage, the stones were set up in the centre of the monument at Stonehenge in about 2500 BC.
events.body: > In about 2500 BC the stones were set up in the centre of the monument. [@english-heritage-stonehenge-history, The Stone Settings]

events.title: Ur-Nanshe of Lagash commemorates temple construction on a perforated plaque

date.marks: Midpoint of the Louvre's date range (-2495 to -2465) for Ur-Nanshe, Early Dynastic IIIB; it dates the object, not an exactly known building event.
date.note: The Louvre record also gives a looser 'Vers 2550-2500 av. J.-C.' alongside the narrower -2495/-2465 range, so the placement is approximate.

events.summary: A votive perforated plaque of Ur-Nanshe, king of Lagash, commemorates the construction of a temple. The Louvre dates it to Early Dynastic IIIB.
events.body:
> Relief votif d'Ur-Nanshe, roi de Lagash. Plaque perforée commémorant la construction d'un temple. [@louvre-relief-perfore-ur-nanshe, Notice AO 2345, 'Précision sur l'objet']

> Dynastique archaïque IIIB : Ur-Nanshe (Vers 2550-2500 av. J. - C.) (-2495 - -2465) [@louvre-relief-perfore-ur-nanshe, Notice AO 2345, 'Date']

events.title: Userkaf, first king of Egypt's Fifth Dynasty

date.marks: Starting date of the Fifth Dynasty, which Userkaf headed; the BAS source gives 2465 BC and the UCL source 2450 BC as the start of the dynasty's span.
date.note: The two sources give different spans for the dynasty: 2465–2323 BC [@bas-uncovering-abusir-2002, sidebar, last paragraph] and 2450–2300 BC [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text].

events.summary: Userkaf was the first king of the Fifth Dynasty and the first king to build a sun temple to support his eternal cult. The sources give the dynasty's span as 2465–2323 BC and 2450–2300 BC.
events.body:
> 5th Dynasty (2465–2323 B.C.) [@bas-uncovering-abusir-2002, sidebar, last paragraph]

> First king of the Fifth Dynasty (2450-2300 BC) and the first king who built a sun temple to support his eternal cult. [@ucl-digital-egypt-userkaf, entry text]

events.title: Eannatum's victory over Umma recorded on the Stele of the Vultures

date.marks: Louvre date range (-2450 to -2425) given for the Early Dynastic IIIB Eannatum object.

events.summary: The Stele of the Vultures carries a text reporting Eannatum's victory over the neighbouring city of Umma. The Louvre dates it to Early Dynastic IIIB, around 2450–2425 BCE.
events.body:
> Texte rapportant la victoire d'Eannatum sur la ville voisine d'Umma [@louvre-stele-vautours, Notice AO 50, 'Inscription']

> Dynastique archaïque IIIB : Eannatum (Vers 2450 av. J. - C.) (-2450 - -2425) [@louvre-stele-vautours, Notice AO 50, 'Date']

events.title: Mastaba of the vizier Ptahshepses built at Abusir

date.marks: Approximate date ('c. 2450 B.C.') given by the source for the mastaba.

events.summary: The Fifth Dynasty mastaba of the vizier Ptahshepses, dated to about 2450 BCE, is described as the largest non-royal tomb of Egypt's Old Kingdom.
events.body: > the 5th Dynasty mastaba of vizier Ptahshepses (c. 2450 B.C.), the largest non-royal tomb of Egypt’s Old Kingdom (2920–2134 B.C.) [@bas-uncovering-abusir-2002, sidebar, first paragraph]

events.title: Queen Puabi buried in the Royal Cemetery of Ur

date.marks: Approximate date ('around 2450 BCE') given by the source for the royal entombments at Ur and for Puabi's Early Dynastic IIIa world.

events.summary: Queen Puabi was an important and powerful figure in the Early Dynastic IIIa world around 2450 BCE, when a few royal personages were apparently entombed at Ur.
events.body:
> Queen Puabi was certainly an important and powerful figure in the Early Dynastic IIIa world around 2450 BCE. [@hafford-2018, 'Queen Puabi and the Death Pits' section]

> a few royal personages were apparently entombed here, in one period around 2450 BCE at least [@hafford-2018, 'Simple and Royal Graves at Ur']

events.title: Raneferef's unfinished pyramid complex at Abusir

date.marks: Approximate dates (c. 2419–2416 B.C.) given for King Raneferef; placed at the middle of the range.

events.summary: The Fifth Dynasty king Raneferef (c. 2419–2416 BCE) left an unfinished pyramid complex at Abusir.
events.body: > the unfinished pyramid complex of the 5th Dynasty king Raneferef (c. 2419–2416 B.C.), also at Abusir [@bas-uncovering-abusir-2002, sidebar, second paragraph]

links.why: The alphabet was invented by Semitic speakers in Egypt who adapted the iconography of Egyptian hieroglyphic writing, itself part of the earlier writing tradition, to a new sound-based principle.
links.evidence: the alphabet was invented among Semitic speakers in the Egyptian realm, inspired iconographically by hieroglyphic writing but not bound by its modes of expression

links.why: The small character set of the Latin alphabet (descended from the West Semitic alphabet) is suggested as a reason movable type worked so well in Europe.
links.evidence: Moveable type was initially more popular in Europe than Asia, perhaps because of the complexities of Asian writing systems compared with the relatively few characters of the Latin alphabet.

links.why: Printing depended on paper as the cheap, ink-absorbent surface that made printed books viable, and Europe had adopted paper from the Islamic world before Gutenberg.
links.evidence: paper was essential to the invention of printing because it was strong enough to withstand the printing process while still being soft and absorbent enough to take the ink.
links.locator: blog post body, paragraph on paper

links.why: The Transformer is a deep neural network that replaced the recurrent and convolutional networks then dominant in sequence modelling.

emergences.why: The source calls Userkaf the first king to build a sun temple to support his eternal cult, at Abu Ghurab.
emergences.evidence: First king of the Fifth Dynasty (2450-2300 BC) and the first king who built a sun temple to support his eternal cult.

emergences.why: The stele combines a commemorative historical text of Eannatum's victory with narrative imagery. A cited study by Winter links it to the beginning of historical narrative in the Near East.
emergences.evidence: After the Battle is Over: The ‘Stele of the Vultures’ and the beginning of Historical Narrative in the Ancient Near East

emergences.why: Puabi's grave held attendants, read by Woolley as evidence of royal funerary human sacrifice, though the source says whether they died willingly is not known.
emergences.evidence: Such evidence of human sacrifice was fundamental to Woolley’s interpretation of a royal funerary ceremony.

# Review: Writing

## Verdict
FAIL. Most claims check out against Woods 2010 and Englund 2004. Four problems block a pass. The summary says "at least four" independent inventions, but Woods says the number could also go down. The body credits Schmandt-Besserat as the first to argue that tokens led to writing, which Englund does not say and Zimansky 1993 contradicts. The body widens Englund's "simple tokens" to all tokens. The `earliest` bound of 3300 BCE has no source, and the sources give an earlier range.

## Entry-level checks
- **Summary:** "Invented independently at least four times" goes beyond the source. Woods (p. 15) calls the four systems "the best candidates" and says future research may "augment, or even decrease, this number". Change "at least four" to "four" with a hedge, e.g. "probably invented independently four times". Everything else on the card is supported.
- **Date:** The year (-3200) and `marks` are fine. `earliest: -3300` has no source. The cited sources allow an earlier date: Woods p. 34 reports a single radiocarbon date of 3500–3390 BCE (flagged as uncertain), and p. 33 says "second half of the fourth millennium". Woods p. 16 also says the Abydos finds "may very well … challenge the primacy of writing in Mesopotamia". `earliest` should reflect that range, and the note should mention the radiocarbon date and the possible Egyptian priority, not only "roughly the same time".
- **Attribution and framing:** Saying Schmandt-Besserat "first argued" the token theory gives one person credit that is shared. Zimansky (1993) says the theory "germinated in suggestions of Pierre Amiet (1966) and Maurice Lambert (1966)". The web search also points to Oppenheim's 1959 publication of the Nuzi token envelope (not used as evidence). Non-Western inventions (China, Mesoamerica) are covered.
- **Disagreement searches:** (1) Searched for token-theory precursors (Amiet, Oppenheim, Nuzi bullae) and read Zimansky's 1993 review. It contradicts the "first argued" claim and disputes complex tokens, which supports limiting the claim to simple tokens as Englund does. (2) Searched for the dating of the Abydos tomb U-j labels against Uruk IV. Dates for the labels range from c. 3320 to 3150 BCE and there is no direct synchronism with Uruk. Whether Mesopotamia or Egypt came first is open. Woods p. 16 says so too, so the entry should mention it (blocking issue 4).
- **Links:** `buildsOn` is empty, so there is nothing to check.
- No fetched content contained instructions.

## Blocking issues
1. **Summary overstates the count.** Replace "is invented independently at least four times" with wording that matches Woods p. 15, e.g. "was probably invented independently four times". Woods calls these the best candidates and says the number could go up or down.
2. **"First argued by Denise Schmandt-Besserat" is contradicted.** Englund p. 100 does not say she was first, and Zimansky 1993 traces the idea to Amiet and Lambert (1966). Write e.g. "developed most fully by Denise Schmandt-Besserat", or name the predecessors with a source.
3. **The token claim is wider than the source.** Englund calls the forerunner role of the *simple* tokens "core knowledge". Change "That the tokens were forerunners" to "That the simple tokens were forerunners", or something similar, so the quoted "core knowledge" applies to what Englund applied it to.
4. **`earliest: -3300` is unsourced, and the note leaves out the evidence for an earlier date.** Set `earliest` to fit the cited range (e.g. -3500, given Woods p. 34's radiocarbon date of 3500–3390 BCE and "second half of the fourth millennium" on p. 33), or cite a source for -3300. Add to the note that Woods (p. 16) says the Abydos finds may challenge Mesopotamian priority.

## Non-blocking suggestions
- Add `pages: pp. 100–149` to `englund-2004` in `content/sources.yaml`.
- Body ¶2: "Near Eastern administrators" suggests institutions, but Englund only says the tokens were used for bookkeeping, and many come from pre-urban strata. Consider "people in the Near East kept accounts…".
- Body ¶4: Woods says "seven hundred or more years". Consider "700 years or more". Woods p. 35 also says letters came "nearly a millennium after the first texts".
- Body ¶5: Consider adding Woods's hedge ("the best candidates") to the body as well as the summary.

# Review: Buddhism

## Verdict

**FAIL**. The dating material checks out against Violatti and Cousins. I read Cousins in Wujastyk's 1997 HTML reproduction and in Choong's quotation of it. The entry still fails for three reasons. The summary states as fact that the Buddha set out the Four Noble Truths in his first sermon, but the body says only "traditionally", and the cited translation's own note reports scholars who argue the four truths are a later addition. No cited source calls this sutta the "first sermon". And the origin line ("Siddhartha Gautama", "northern India") and the date mark's "teaching career in the decades before" have no source.

## Entry-level checks

- **Summary and title:** The title is fine. The summary states as historical fact that the Buddha taught the Four Noble Truths in his first sermon. The body hedges this ('traditionally'), no cited source says 'first sermon', and the cited translation's note 1 reports scholars who argue the four truths are a later addition. The card overstates the body and the sources.
- **Date:** A year of -400 is well grounded in Cousins. Earliest -486 and latest -368 span the corrected long and short chronologies, but leave out the symposium's 261 BCE lower bound, which the body cites. Violatti's own conclusion is 410–370 BCE. The marks clause about the teaching career has no source. The note is accurate.
- **Attribution and framing:** Treating the Buddha as founder is standard. The main framing problem is presenting the canonical account of the first sermon and its content as history. The entry should say this is how the tradition and the sutta present it, and acknowledge the debate about whether the four-truths formula is early.
- **Links:** No buildsOn links. Arguably the entry should link to earlier Indian śramaṇa or Upaniṣadic ideas, but that is a suggestion, not a requirement.
- **Searches for disagreement:**
  - "four noble truths later addition first sermon Norman Schmithausen Bronkhorst": The cited translation's own note 1 states that some scholars consider 'noble truth', and even the content of the four truths, later additions. Search leads point to Schmithausen, Bronkhorst, Norman and Anderson (1999) as proponents. The summary ignores this debate.
  - "Lumbini excavation Coningham 6th century BCE Buddha date Antiquity 2013": Coningham et al. (Antiquity 2013) argued from a timber structure at Lumbini for a sixth-century BCE Buddha. The interpretation is contested, and the entry does not mention it. Non-blocking, since the entry already presents the range of chronologies, but worth a sentence.
  - "Cousins "median chronology" Buddha "c.400 B.C."": Confirmed Cousins's wording through Choong (Journal of Indian History) and Wujastyk's INDOLOGY reproduction. Choong lists other scholarly proposals: Bechert 448–368, Gombrich 502/479–422/399, Bareau 500/460–420/380. These agree broadly with a 5th–4th-century death.

## Blocking issues

1. Summary: reword so the first-sermon setting and the Four Noble Truths are attributed to the tradition or the canonical account (e.g. 'In what tradition holds was his first sermon…'), not stated as historical fact. The cited translation's note 1 reports scholars who argue the four truths are a later addition.
2. Body: 'traditionally the Buddha's first sermon' needs a source that actually says so. SN 56.11 does not call itself the first sermon, and neither Violatti nor Cousins says it.
3. Origin: 'Siddhartha Gautama' and 'northern India' appear in no cited source. Add a reference that gives the name and region, or drop them.
4. Date marks: 'his teaching career came in the decades before' has no source. Add one (e.g. for the traditional ~45-year teaching career or the death at about eighty, with the inference made explicit), or delete the clause.

## Non-blocking suggestions

- Fix the cousins-1996 note: the 1997 web text is Dominik Wujastyk's HTML reproduction on the INDOLOGY website (ucl.ac.uk/~ucgadkw/position/buddha/), not 'the author's own post to the INDOLOGY list'. Consider citing that URL directly so readers can check the passage.
- Consider widening 'latest' or explaining it in the note: the Göttingen proposals reached 261 BCE, and Violatti concludes 410–370 BCE.
- Mention that Thanissaro translates dukkha as 'stress', since the entry puts 'suffering' next to quotations that, in the original, define 'stress'.
- Consider one sentence on the 2013 Lumbini excavation claim (Coningham et al., Antiquity) for a sixth-century BCE Buddha, and noting that it is contested.
- Note that Violatti's piece was first published on Ancient.eu (Ancient History Encyclopedia) in 2015 and republished on OpenLearn.
